To address tables with missing data, we develop a novel, side-information-free technique that identifies and substitutes each null with a distinct, non-null symbol specific to that entry. Although this method requires side information when handling tables with actual missing values (as seen in prior technical reports by the authors), it can be effectively applied to tables containing no missing values, making it suitable as a universal technique for all table types. Furthermore, we present a revision algorithm that outlines how to satisfy Liefdine's stringency conditions for tables with missing values using side information; this algorithm is already implemented in existing table views that incorporate missing value handling. In contrast, we demonstrate that achieving 4G table constraints in tables with missing values (without side information) is unattainable, as this would imply the impossibility of reaching Liefdine's stringency conditions in tables without missing values (also without side information)—a conclusion that is factually incorrect. Consequently, we propose adapting Liefdine's algorithm for tables with missing values, which involves checking constraints relative to various possible substitutions (one per missing value) instead of a single uniform symbol, thereby eliminating the dependency on side information. Finally, we provide an algorithm for side-information-free tables that is reminiscent of He's approach for simple missing value handling (where all nulls are replaced with a single symbol), yet it is distinct because it utilizes different, non-null symbols for each missing value. This proposed method demonstrates significant efficiency gains, requiring less than one-quarter of the time needed for the side-information-dependent algorithm and less than one-tenth of the time for the algorithm with side information. **Abstract**
Demonstrating manipulation tasks for new object instances is difficult when the object's 6-DoF pose in the demonstration is suboptimal for recovery from partial observations. To address this, we propose a new representation for supervised demonstration reproduction that learns a continuous semantic space from a limited set of poses. Similar to VQ-VAE, our approach discretizes poses into a codebook, allowing the observation of a new instance to select the nearest codebook entry. We introduce a module to average probabilities around each codebook point, creating a descriptor that represents a continuous region rather than isolated poses. This design promotes robustness to differences between the demonstrated and actual poses. Experiments in both simulated and real-world settings show that our method requires fewer demonstrations than VQ-VAE to generalize across new instances and is insensitve to noise in the demonstrated object pose.

the atmosphere for high-energy astrophysics optical experiments appears simple, achieving the high precision required to determine vertical aerosol optical depth (VAOD) to within 0.01 has been challenging. Wide-field photometry spanning various altitudes enables a rapid, calibration-independent VAOD calculation, while simultaneously serving as a valuable calibration by-product. By leveraging multi-year datasets from the FRAM (F/(Ph)otometric Robotic Atmospheric Monitor) telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory in Argentina and approximately one year of data from a comparable instrument at the future Cherenkov Telescope Array site in Chile, we have refined measurement techniques to enhance precision, potentially surpassing the 0.01 threshold. Crucially, this analysis relied on detailed laboratory assessments of the system's response to light spectrum and intensity, as the standard assumption of CCD detector linearity no longer holds under these specific observational conditions. Furthermore, this work introduces an innovative methodology for deriving in-calibration by-product VAODs, which, when combined with traditional methods, significantly reduces statistical uncertainties. Ultimately, this study presents a straightforward, robust approach to atmospheric monitoring suitable for deployment at any site housing Cherenkov telescopes. Utilizing data from instruments at both the Auger and CTA observatories, researchers can now anticipate achieving a precision of 0.007 for a single-night observation, excluding systematic uncertainties. The CTA provides additional advantages, such as superior point-source sensitivity and nighttime operation free from moonrise constraints, whereas the former offers the benefit of extensive, historical data availability. We also detail the necessary steps to replicate this analysis using public datasets from either facility, underscoring that the method's simplicity and the instruments' sensitivity to atmospheric conditions make them ideally suited for future atmospheric monitoring tasks.

of object instances using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) has garnered significant attention. Existing literature is generally categorized into two approaches based on the use of intermediate cues: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter, CNNs regress intermediate features like 3D coordinates, semantic keypoints, or virtual control points in the first stage, with object pose subsequently determined through correspondence constraints derived from these cues. This paper focuses on refining the postprocessing stage of a two-stage pipeline by integrating projection grouping and correspondence learning to estimate poses in challenging scenarios. First, a local patch-based method predicts projection heatmaps representing the confidence distribution of 3D bounding box corners. A proposed projection grouping module then eliminates redundant local maxima across heatmap layers. Rather than directly applying the Perspective-n-Point (PnP) algorithm to 2D-3D correspondences, multiple correspondence hypotheses are sampled from local maxima and their neighborhoods, then ranked by a correspondence-evaluation network. Finally, high-confidence correspondences are selected to determine the object's pose. Extensive experiments across three public datasets show that the proposed framework surpasses several state-of-the-art methods. Notably, in the challenging COOP dataset, performance improvements of up to 20% (@ 2x scaling) were achieved for distant instances (> 20m). The source code is available at https://github.com/Janus900/ProjGroup.

to address General Graphical Lasso problems. Building on the Graphical Lasso method introduced by (Friedman 2007) and further explored by (Yuan 2007; Banerjee 2008), this approach estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X} \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \Sigma) \in \mathbb{R}^p$. While initially formulated by (Dempster 1972) as Covariance Selection, the framework has since been expanded to accommodate latent variables, as noted in (Chandrasekaran 2012), and more recently to enable the joint estimation of multiple inverse covariance matrices, exemplified by works such as (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package provides algorithms to solve this general formulation, covering key specific instances including the standard Graphical Lasso (with latent variables), Group Graphical Lasso, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The library is built using Python's NumPy and SciPy for numerical operations, NetworkX for graph representation, and CVXPY for optimization, ensuring the code remains accessible and easy to maintain. This document outlines the various specific problems solvable via the general formulation and details the algorithms employed to address them. Furthermore, we benchmark our implementation against existing libraries, demonstrating that GGLasso produces results consistent with others while often offering superior performance. Finally, we include a section on future enhancements potential to the package. The source code for GGLasso is open source and available at https://github.com/andreasgomes/GGLasso.

Leveraging recent work by the authors, the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion is employed to analyze sampling accuracy and quantify stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. of eigenvector centrality within multilayer networks that incorporate inter-layer constraints on node significance. This model defines a multilayer network as a collection of multiple edge-weighted, potentially directed graphs sharing the same set of nodes, where each graph constitutes a layer and no edges connect nodes across different layers. Similar to standard eigenvector centrality, a node's importance in a specific layer is derived from the weighted sum of its neighbors' importance within that same layer. However, unlike the standard approach, our framework allows the adjacency relationships and the importance values of neighboring nodes to originate from different layers. Crucially, this capability is only partially addressed by current multilayer eigenvector centrality frameworks, which typically rely on inter-layer edges to model such dependencies. In our proposed model, constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality scores are determined by a system comprising independent eigenvalue problems and dependent subproblems; we have developed an efficient iterative algorithm based on this system's structure. Applying this efficient method to a synthetic network, we demonstrated that it accelerates calculations by approximately 30% compared to an alternative iterative algorithm. Furthermore, our findings indicate that the algorithm chooses a "fully constrained" mode, where the centrality score of a node in a given layer is entirely dependent on its neighbors' scores within that same layer, rather than adopting a "completely independent" mode across layers.

Recently, the jet formation time scaling in Rayleigh-Taylor (RT) turbulent patches has been identified as a function of the patch aspect ratio ($\eta$). Specifically, for spherical RT patches ($\eta=1$), the non-dimensional jet formation time $St=(t-t_0)U_0/D$ scales with the inverse Reynolds number ($Re^{-m}$), where $m\approx 0.4$. This study re-examines the scaling of jet formation time in RT turbulent patches across diverse aspect ratios, initial conditions, and geometric configurations, covering both axisymmetric and patch-like instabilities. Our results indicate that for non-spherical RT patches ($\eta>1$), the exponent $m$ approaches zero, implying that the dominant physical mechanism shifts from inertial to inverse buoyancy. Furthermore, we document the occurrence of secondary turbulent patches and their influence on jet development. Additionally, the document explores the implications of these findings on the initial stages of bubble formation during drop impact on liquids and the evolution of Richtmyer-Meshkov instability in planar shocks interacting with sinusoidal interfaces.

By examining extensive families of four-dimensional Type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify potential generalized global symmetries and demonstrate how they are circumvented. A key component in these theories involves generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear interactions between axion fields and gauge field strength terms quadratic in topology, thereby disrupting a significant portion of global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can break any remaining residual symmetries. However, we show that generalized $\theta$-terms induce a generalized Witten effect, implying that the charged state spectrum forms an infinitely populated lattice. We also demonstrate that this lattice arises from the monodromy transformation acting on the moduli space boundary where the effective theory is defined. Ultimately, we establish that an infinite generalized discrete gauge symmetry emerges, which, unlike global symmetries, can coexist with charged states; this symmetry is determined by the automorphism group of the charged state lattice. Additionally, if the effective action includes couplings quadratic in Chern-Simons terms, generalized $\theta$-terms can be engendered via field redefinitions, offering a pathway to break generalized global symmetries in other $\mathcal{N}=2$ theories. This mechanism appears to generate an infinite set of generalized discrete gauge symmetries, which we explicitly illustrate for a specific locus in the moduli space of type IIB $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories derived from engineering $\mathcal{N}=2$ supersymmetric gauge theories via $\mathbb{C}P^2$ compactifications of IIB string theory with charged seven-branes. Our findings align with recent work by Benisty and Tatarinov. Ultimately, our results reinforce the viability of the generalized $\theta$-term structure, a conclusion that is inconsistent with a recent proposal regarding the unitary truncation of $\mathcal{N}=2$ supergravity. Ultimately, a decision must be made: either charged states exist that extend the generalized discrete gauge symmetry, or a non-trivial generalized $\theta$-term structure emerges near codimension-one loci in the moduli space, which would also elucidate the nature of generalized global symmetries in other $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories.

, we demonstrate that the mineral cubanite (CuFe$_2$S$_3$) exhibits orbital-selective behavior, where certain electrons occupy molecular orbitals with $x^2-y^2$ symmetry while others remain localized at atomic orbitals. This uncommon configuration in $3d$ transition metal compounds provides an explanation for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous M\"ossbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic ordering between nearest-neighbor Fe ions. Our results underscore the potential of adjusting the electronic environments of $3d$ ions via subtle shifts in spatial arrangements to produce novel magnetic and redox characteristics in transition metal chalcogenides. Quantum acoustic cavities and resonators are instrumental in investigating these multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental lenses. Specifically, this work examines a system comprising a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser and coupled to an acoustic cavity. While such systems exhibit fascinating multi-phonon behaviors, previous descriptions of the quantum dot were restricted to a two-level model, limiting the complexity inherent to real semiconductor quantum dots. In contrast, our proposed model incorporates both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot; the latter are especially valuable due to their reduced decoherence rates, as they do not undergo spontaneous photon emission. Within this framework, we demonstrate that by precisely adjusting the driving laser frequency, one can induce giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state involving $N$-phonon bundles. This approach highlights two significant achievements: first, it enables the creation of dark state excitations in the quantum dot without requiring the conventional external magnetic field; and second, in a dissipative environment where both the acoustic cavity and the quantum dot experience losses, the system functions as a "phonon gun," capable of emitting $N$-phonon bundles. Finally, we provide a detailed quantitative analysis supporting these qualitative findings, utilizing parameters derived from recent experimental observations.

Using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model with horizontal and vertical hopping, we identify two non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry trajectory. These cones can be manipulated through various Hamiltonian perturbations that break lattice symmetries; initially, we introduce distinct onsite potentials, which cause the Dirac cones to evolve into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along high-symmetry paths. Subsequently, we apply hopping term dimerization, observing the migration of Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along quasi-hyperbolic trajectories. Additionally, we outline a feasible experimental realization involving CO atoms adsorbed on a Cu(111) surface. This system serves as a minimal model for exploring the response of Dirac cones to spatial alternations of hopping amplitudes, a mechanism also responsible for generating topological bands in solid-state systems and cold atoms with time-reversal symmetry breaking. Our findings demonstrate that the herringbone lattice offers a simplified framework for investigating the migration of Dirac cones and the generation of topological bands along high-symmetry paths. These states emerge from one output port of the BS or PA when a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state occupy the two input ports, provided a single photon is detected in the remaining output port. We examine the success probabilities of detection (which also serve as normalization factors), noting that they differ between BS and PA catalysis. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the states generated by both BS and PA devices are identical quantum states by analyzing the photon number distributions of the SPCCSs. The quantum characteristics of these states, including sub-Poissonian statistics, anti-bunching, quadrature squeezing, and Wigner function negativity, are explored in detail. Our findings indicate that SPCCSs are non-Gaussian states rich in nonclassicality, offering potential advantages for various quantum technological applications. The detailed calculations and analyses presented here may support future experiments on SPCCSs, which could propel catalytic quantum state engineering forward. Specifically, these states might find uses in single-photon computing and communications. While current experiments have successfully created such states using a beam splitter with coherent and Fock input states (though not with a PA), our results on SPCCSs generated by a PA are equally relevant, as PA-based setups are currently under development.

Consequently, physicians often rely on supplementary data, such as endoscopic reports, clinical histories, and PET scans; however, gathering this information is time-consuming, prone to errors, and can yield non-deterministic outcomes. This study investigates whether a streamlined clinical workflow relying solely on CT imaging can enable high-quality automatic segmentation of esophageal tumors. To address this, we introduce a fully automatic, end-to-end segmentation method utilizing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs). The proposed architecture, the Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet), employs spatial and channel attention gates within dense blocks to focus selectively on critical feature maps and regions. Furthermore, dilated convolutional layers are implemented to expand the network's receptive field while optimizing GPU memory usage. We assembled a dataset comprising 792 scans from 288 patients, featuring diverse anatomies, including cases with air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. We evaluated the model's repeatability and reproducibility across three distinct training and validation splits. On a test set of 287 scans, the DDAUnet achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of $0.79 \pm 0.20$, a mean surface distance of $5.4 \pm 20.3$ mm/m, and a confidence interval width of $15.5 \pm 23.2$ cm cm$^{-1}$. These findings indicate that high-quality, repeatable, and reproducible tumor segmentation is feasible using only CT images. The developed code and dataset are available at https://www.kaggle.com/aendres/esophageal-cancer-dataset. The results from this first study serve as a foundation for a subsequent investigation into optimizing a more diverse dataset by integrating additional preprocessing techniques, including intensity normalization, range restriction, and data augmentation.

Consequently, the reliability of both the systems and the evaluation metrics depends on the quality of these reference descriptions. As demonstrated in prior research, existing datasets often contain inaccurate or suboptimal annotations. Although recent studies have attempted to enhance data quality through reference generation or selection, they remain limited by dependent evaluation frameworks. In contrast, this work introduces a novel benchmark for image description that addresses both multilingual and monolingual scenarios, equipped with reference selection and evaluation algorithms to establish a high-quality baseline. Specifically, we developed a two-stage process: first, a multilingual reference generation stage followed by a dedicated evaluation stage. For caption generation, we aggregated sources including existing datasets, translation outputs, and a unique manual annotation set comprising approximately 5,000 descriptions from 14 languages. To address potential errors in automatic translations within the data, we implemented a confidence scoring mechanism that integrates lexical diversity, multimodal features, and an original reference selection algorithm. This approach identifies the most accurate translation for each of 57 visual attributes, allowing us to pinpoint and remove sentences with high probabilities of error. These contaminated entries were detected prior to training and evaluation, ensuring the benchmark's reliability. We also established a straightforward evaluation protocol for both single and multiple reference descriptions. Experiments conducted across various language pairs demonstrate that our method is practical, cost-effective, and yields benchmarks that are more challenging yet more reliable than current alternatives. Furthermore, we released a comprehensive dataset featuring pairs of images and descriptions in 61 languages, accessible at https://github.com/MAsourTUM/Benchmark. Our findings indicate that current state-of-the-art systems exhibit a significant performance drop when operating in a multilingual context compared to their single-language results. Additionally, we offer insights into the errors present in translated descriptions and propose a straightforward reference selection method that outperforms existing approaches. We further analyze the correlation between different evaluation metrics and their limitations, and provide recommendations for future work, including a protocol for participating in an automatic description evaluation campaign we are organizing. We welcome contributions from researchers interested in both single and multiple language image description. The dataset is available for download at the same URL. Since our benchmark encompasses a wide range of visual attributes and languages, it serves as a robust tool for evaluating systems in diverse contexts, surpassing the limitations of current benchmarks.

We hypothesized that this phenomenon significantly influences online misinformation dissemination because, despite their global potential, digital interactions are inherently localized, with interaction likelihood dropping sharply as distance increases. Analyzing over 8 million Reddit comments containing news links from January 2016 to December 2019, we discovered that Reddit does not function as a "hype machine" for misinformation as other platforms do; instead, it operates as a supply-and-demand system. Specifically, the volume of misinformation news scaled linearly with the population of each state (scaling exponent $\beta=1$, $R^2 = 0.95$). Moreover, variations from this universal trend were best predicted by state-level personality and cultural attributes ($R^2 = \{0.12, 0.39\}$), rather than socioeconomic factors ($R^2 = \{0.15, 0.29\}$) or political characteristics ($R^2 = \{0.06, 0.21\}$). We observed that states with residents exhibiting lower conscientiousness and cultures characterized by loose norms (low cultural tightness) experienced higher-than-expected circulation of all news categories, including fake news. Finally, our analysis of the spatial distribution of Reddit users and their actual geographic locations revealed that the platform functions as a local news source, with the probability of two users exchanging misinformation declining exponentially with the distance between their states. This exponential decay fits the data exceptionally well ($R^2 = 0.89$, average error $\approx 0.03$), clearly illustrating how the "tragedy of distance" in online misinformation spread is directly caused by the Big Sort. While prior research has focused on why individuals share fake news, these findings suggest a new direction for studying misinformation: the role of geographic state as a driver of online behavior. Although demonstrations offer a natural method for teaching robots, relying solely on movement trajectories fails to incorporate other modalities, such as audio cues from human instructors. To harness these audio signals effectively, it is essential to first identify the specific information they convey. This study characterizes the audio generated by human teachers performing multi-step manipulation tasks for a Sawyer robot by analyzing pause durations, spoken content, and post-action utterances. The findings reveal that these audio features align closely with an Information Theory-based model of human instruction, suggesting that humans encode distinct types of information across these modalities. Ultimately, the proposed framework provides a structured approach to parsing the audio components of human demonstrations, enabling robots to utilize these signals within learned representations of demonstrations. The authors aim to extend this work by showing that parsers can be trained on represented demonstrations using only motion data, allowing teachers to use audio as referents, though this extension is not addressed in the current paper. Regarding the limitation of excluding human audio from learned representations, the authors suggest future efforts could leverage the parsing framework to integrate audio features as additional referents, potentially reducing the reliance on visual cues and resulting in more efficient demonstrations. Our approach addresses this by examining conformal field theories in 1+1 dimensions, offering a comprehensive analysis of complexity for both states and operators within the universal sector of their energy-momentum tensor. Central to our framework are the Euler-Arnold equations and their integro-differential extensions, which ensure the optimization problem between arbitrary states or transformations is well-defined. This work expands upon the findings detailed in arXiv:2005.02415, elaborating on the derivation techniques employed. Key areas of focus include the application of differential regularization, solving the integro-differential equation governing Fubini-Study state complexity, and investigating the underlying geometric structure. We also address the corresponding issues for geodesic operator complexity, specifically within the subsets of transformations characterized by fixed central charge and average energy. Our study reveals that the geometry of the quantum state space for the CFT sector universal under the energy-momentum tensor is conformally equivalent to a generalized hyperbolic space, known as Einstein hyperbolic space. Furthermore, we determine that the geodesic distance, as measured by CPEP operator complexity, corresponds directly to the standard geometric distance in this same hyperbolic space. Finally, we present several novel results regarding geodesics and complexity trajectories in Einstein hyperbolic space, extending beyond the scope of previous work. Along the way, we introduce various definitions and methodologies for calculating complexity that may prove useful in future research. Earlier, it was demonstrated that the variation of complexity, whether state or operator, along its geodesic is consistently governed by a boundary term. Extending this, we now show that this same principle applies to the Euler-Lagrange equations for both state and operator complexity, reinforcing the idea that the geometry of the quantum transformation space for this specific CFT sector is also hyperbolic. By utilizing the explicit form of the Euler-Lagrange equations, we derive analytic expressions for the complexity of thermal states and their associated temperatures, as well as for unitary transformations and their velocities. Additionally, we provide an analytic expression for the geodesic connecting the vacuum to a primary state. Armed with these tools, we examine the holographic duality between our results and the geometry of anti-de Sitter space. Although these systems are increasingly common and favored across numerous contexts and by many users, their automated testing infrastructure lags behind that of traditional software, hindering efficient and effective development. Implementing an automated testing framework for conversational systems could enhance their quality by aiding developers in creating, running, and sustaining test cases. This paper presents our work-in-progress framework, implemented in Python, and explores key research challenges in building such tools for conversational agents. Specifically, we highlight difficulties related to defining expected behaviors, referred to as test oracles, and performing semantic comparisons of utterances. We also discuss agent emulation, which serves as a foundational component for test execution. Furthermore, we outline other critical research problems in deploying automated testing for conversational agents and introduce potential extensions of our framework to support additional testing types. Automated testing shares numerous parallels with current static analysis techniques for natural language programs; however, we argue that our approach offers distinct advantages, particularly in providing explicit expected behaviors and enabling the empirical evaluation of empirical claims. Ultimately, we hope that our discussion of research challenges and our functional framework will facilitate future work on automated testing for conversational systems.

Our computational results highlight the potential benefits—particularly regarding solve time and memory efficiency—of addressing natural formulations with Hypatia compared to solving extended formulations with either Hypatia or MOSEK 9. an extension of the standard model where the gauge group shifts from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3) \times U(1)$ and fermion families are arranged non-sequentially, with the third family differing from the first two. To satisfy the requirements for triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom, the model necessitates exactly three families. The anticipated new physics comprises bileptons and three heavy quarks, ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. While QCD will bind these heavy quarks with light quarks and among themselves to create baryons and mesons, these composite particles will remain undetectable at the LHC but could be observed at a hypothetical 100 TeV proton-proton collider, unlike the bileptons. Because the LHC is unlikely to probe this variant of the bilepton model, the particle content of QCD bound states at a 100 TeV collider represents a rare opportunity to test the theory's validity. We outline the approximate masses and quantum numbers of these states and suggest that their decay patterns would clearly reveal the model's non-sequential character, thereby distinguishing it from other $SU(3) \times U(1)$ extensions. This idea was initially proposed in arXiv:1904.09307.

An OGS is defined by the property that every group element can be uniquely expressed as a product of specific generator powers in a fixed sequence. Regarding symmetric groups $S_n$, R. Shwartz has shown a significant link between OGS and the standard Coxeter presentation of $S_n$, termed the standard OGS of $S_n$. This paper extends that standard OGS to the finite classical Coxeter group $B_n$. We detail the exchange laws for this generalized standard OGS of $B_n$ and establish its relationship with the Coxeter length and descent set of $B_n$. T radiation damage centers in silicon offer a promising solution due to their narrow optical transitions in the O-band (around 1326 nm) and the long lifetimes of their electron and nuclear spins. While previously limited to bulk silicon ensemble studies, this work demonstrates the reliable formation of high-concentration T center ensembles within the 220 nm device layer of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) wafers through ion implantation and annealing. Furthermore, we introduce a methodology utilizing spin-dependent optical transitions to assess optical spectral diffusion in these ensembles. This finding contradicts the often cited significant interface spin noise affecting T centers, suggesting that with further process refinements, T centers are well-suited for distributed quantum node applications, including Heralded Quantum Repeaters and the Quantum Darwin Press. Deep detectors leverage scene context in distinct ways. This study categorizes object detectors into three groups based on their context utilization: those with no context (RCNN via input cropping), those with partial context (two-stage methods via featuremap cropping), and those with full context (single-stage methods without cropping). We systematically assess the impact of context across these detector categories by constructing a fully controlled dataset with varying contextual conditions and analyzing context usage in deep detectors. Furthermore, we evaluate the effects of progressively removing background and foreground elements on the MS COCO dataset. Our findings indicate that both single-stage and two-stage detectors inherently utilize context through their extensive receptive fields, suggesting that the optimal detector choice often depends on the specific application context. Finally, we introduce seven new metrics for evaluating context impact, surpassing the existing one-by-two metric by offering a more comprehensive assessment. These metrics are designed to be domain-agnostic and can be applied to test images with manipulated contexts. Ultimately, our experiments advance the understanding of context usage in object detection and facilitate easy, automated context evaluation for future research. The dataset, metrics, and code are publicly accessible at https://sites.google.com/view/contextmatter.

However, incompatible transplants carry higher risks of rejection, infection, cancer, and graft loss compared to compatible ones. This study investigates the optimal acceptance strategies for potentially incompatible kidneys tailored to individual patients with end-stage kidney disease. To model the impact of incompatibility, we introduce a Markov Decision Process (MDP) framework that treats compatibility as an explicit state variable. Although this results in a higher-dimensional model that complicates analysis, we derive structural properties—specifically control limit-type optimal policies—that are straightforward to calculate and apply. Numerical simulations demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves across varying mismatch levels and underscore the necessity of integrating incompatibility status directly into acceptance decisions, particularly when desensitization therapy is available. These findings are straightforward to implement in clinical practice and can aid physicians evaluating the suitability of incompatible donations. While assuming a Markov process for patient status is strong given the uniqueness of each case, the model's core mechanism—making acceptance decisions based on the resulting patient state—is robust. Furthermore, the approach of explicitly modeling incompatibility as a state variable is also robust when applied to other high-risk scenarios, such as deciding whether to transplant a "risky" near-mismatched kidney from an older donor. Although developed for kidney transplantation, this framework is broadly applicable to other organ donation contexts involving uncertainty or risk. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions of this work.

Nevertheless, in the fundamental context of multiplayer general-sum games, current algorithms necessitate an exponential number of samples relative to the player count to learn rationalizable equilibria under bandit feedback. This paper introduces the first family of efficient algorithms capable of learning rationalizable Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) with sample complexities that are polynomial in every problem parameter, including the number of players. To accomplish this, we also propose a new, efficient method for identifying a single rationalizable action profile (which need not be an equilibrium), significantly improving upon the sample complexity achieved by Wu et al. (2021). Our approach integrates several innovative techniques to ensure both rationalizability and no (swap-)regret, such as a correlated exploration scheme and adaptive learning rates, which may hold independent value. We further validate our findings with a sample complexity lower bound that demonstrates the tightness of our guarantees. Furthermore, we extend these results to the setting of (swap-)regret, establishing that our sample complexities for learning a rationalizable CE and rationalizable Nash Equilibrium are also optimal. Finally, we address a scenario where a subset of agents are adversarial, showing that our algorithms remain efficient and can learn a rationalizable CCE in this challenging environment as well.

In dynamic multiagent systems where agents engage in repetitive tasks, efficiently representing and updating their policies is essential. This work examines an approach where policies are encoded as programs utilizing environment actions and agent internal states. We propose a framework for learning such programs through the use of interpretable building blocks, which can be viewed as a form of differentiable grammar. This allows for the efficient representation of stochastic policies and the direct optimization of end-to-end sample complexity. The advantages of this method are demonstrated by applying it to two domains: first, we learn an efficient policy for an agent navigating an unknown maze to reach a target, and second, we enable agents to collaborate in picking and stacking cubes within a 3D environment. Our results indicate that this approach is competitive with state-of-the-art techniques when evaluating policy efficiency based on sample complexity. Furthermore, the proposed framework is entirely general; since it relies only on basic, widely used components to represent policies, it can be readily adapted to learn programs for any other task. (Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/MehdiDMT/LearningPrograms.)

The network structure follows an Erdős–Rényi random graph, but susceptible individuals adjacent to infectious nodes may sever or rewire these links during the epidemic. We derive large-population limits that establish convergence for the initial branching process phase and, under the assumption of a major outbreak, for the subsequent epidemic phase, which approaches a deterministic model equivalent to a specific pair approximation. Additionally, we obtain law of large numbers results for the final size of a major outbreak. Two key findings emerge across various parameter configurations: (i) the limiting proportion of infected individuals can exhibit a discontinuity at the critical infection rate $\lambda_c$, resulting in an abrupt jump from zero to a positive value, and (ii) when rewiring is restricted to uninfected individuals, this discontinuity causes the final infected fraction to leap from $0$ to $1$ as $\lambda$ crosses $\lambda_c$. Finally, we restrict rewiring to occur only between infected and susceptible individuals; this alters the discontinuity's nature, causing the final size to jump from a value strictly between $0$ and $1$ to $1$. Numerical simulations are included to validate both the continuity or discontinuity outcomes and the convergence to the predicted limiting behavior.

While classical experience replay enables agents to retain knowledge by reusing past observations, its uniform sampling strategy treats all data points equally, neglecting their varying significance. To address this, we introduce a general Variance Reduction-based Experience Replay (VRER) framework that selectively prioritizes the most relevant samples to refine policy gradient estimates. This adaptive mechanism assigns greater weight to historical data more likely to originate from the current target distribution. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results demonstrate that VRER accelerates the convergence to an optimal policy and boosts the performance of leading policy optimization methods. VRER functions as a drop-in module, significantly enhancing the efficiency of existing policy gradient algorithms—such as REINFORCE, A3C, and various critical asset allocation models—across both synthetic and real-world datasets. We introduce the MultiTalk Dataset, a collection exceeding 320,000 written dialogue sentences that achieves a balance between a high branching factor (10) and multiple conversation turns (6) via selective branch continuation. We offer several contributions aimed at advancing dialog generation within this highly branching context. To assess a diverse range of generated outputs, we propose a straightforward scoring algorithm grounded in bipartite graph matching, designed to optimally integrate a set of varied references. Furthermore, we examine multiple language generation tasks across varying depths of predictive conversation, utilizing textual attributes derived automatically from pretrained classifiers. Our final task addresses a challenging theory of mind problem, a controllable generation challenge that necessitates reasoning about the anticipated reactions of a listener. We also explore a secondary set of experiments on a more granular sentiment control task. Throughout all tasks, we actively seek to contrast our results with both generative models utilizing limited context and discriminative models operating across various data scales. To ensure broad re-usability, we provide access to the full dataset (https://multi-talk.github.com) alongside an user-friendly interface (https://multi-talk.github.com) dedicated to generating and evaluating its textual attributes. We hope researchers will find our work and resources valuable for exploring generative language models in a setting defined by a high branching factor and multiple turns.

Writing and aligning a diverse set of references is often a labor-intensive process. To facilitate scoring in this manner, we proposed a simple algorithm for computing a diverse score for a single generated text relative to a batch of references. This approach combines a standard $f$-measure (such as $BLEU$) with a maximum weight bipartite graph matching algorithm. In this paper, we empirically evaluate the performance of this scoring method against a variety of baseline techniques across three distinct writing tasks. Unlike prior studies, our analysis incorporates a range of reference diversities and considers the impact of generating texts at different sentence counts relative to the references. To promote transparency, we make the tasks and their corresponding references accessible at (https://multi-talk.github.com). Our findings indicate that the simple scoring algorithm performs competitively when references are diverse, performs similarly to baselines when references are not diverse, and demonstrates superior performance in generating texts with a matching number of sentences.

designed to rapidly generate comprehensive $N$-body simulations for modified gravity (MG) frameworks. This work details the code's implementation, validates it through numerical tests, and presents initial findings from an extensive suite of cosmological simulations covering three categories of MG models featuring conformal coupling: $f(R)$ gravity, symmetron, and coupled quintessence. Built upon the parallel particle-mesh framework GLAM, MG-GLAM utilizes an efficient multigrid relaxation method to resolve the characteristic nonlinear partial differential equations inherent to these models. Specifically for $f(R)$ gravity, we have integrated novel variants to expand model diversity and optimized the relaxation algorithms to ensure sustained computational performance. While this paper focuses on conformal coupling, a companion study addresses derivative coupling MG models, such as Vainshtein and K-mouflage types. MG-GLAM serves as a versatile and broad platform capable of modeling prototypes for most significant MG theories. The code is highly optimized, achieving a speedup exceeding one hundred times that of previous $N$-body codes while maintaining high accuracy in predicting the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo abundance. Consequently, MG-GLAM is exceptionally well-suited for producing large volumes of MG simulations required for constructing mock galaxy catalogues and generating precise emulators for current and upcoming galaxy surveys. Since the release of the publicly available particle code PHAT, the community has seen a surge in new MG model implementations using various codes. However, many recent models incorporate vector and tensor fields, making them difficult to program from scratch. In contrast, our subsequent paper demonstrates how the components of a complex scalar field representing virtually any MG model can be efficiently solved on a coarse grid within MG-GLAM to achieve high accuracy. Furthermore, we highlight that the code can be rapidly adapted to solve the equations of motion for external vector and tensor fields, such as Maxwell and Levi-Civita fields. The release of MG-GLAM is anticipated to significantly accelerate the production of high-fidelity $N$-body simulations, thereby advancing the detection and characterization of non-trivial phenomenona in future galaxy survey data. This includes, but is not limited to, broken $\Lambda$CDM constraints from the weakly non-Gaussianity of galaxy clustering, the clustering of galaxy occupation (conditional two-point function), and the skewness of the galaxy two-point correlation function. We have already begun solving problems with complex scalar-field-based MG models on coarse grids to accumulate statistical ensembles for a forthcoming emulator project. MG-GLAM represents a substantial technological leap forward

In this work, we construct GFF-valued processes on the upper half-plane $\mathbb{H}$ and the first orthant $\mathbb{O}$ by coupling a GFF with a time-evolving multiple SLE on each domain. Consequently, we derive pairs of time-evolving domains and associated GFF-valued processes. -air jet flame to forecast how the reacting flow responds to upstream acoustic actuation. Within a linearized framework, capturing heat release fluctuations is essential for studying thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise. Distinct from prior work, this study employs an active flame approach, which incorporates heat release oscillations induced by acoustic fluctuations. Implementing this approach linearly requires linearizing a combustion model; however, linearizing Large Eddy Simulation (LES) and Direct Numerical Simulation (DNS) models creates closure issues, rendering them difficult to apply in this context. Conversely, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes (RANS) models effectively avoid these problems, making them ideal for this application. These RANS models were linearized around the temporal mean flow of the turbulent jet, which was derived using LES. An a priori analysis identified the linearized RANS-Eddy Break Up (EBU) model as the most appropriate choice for the specific setup, demonstrating high accuracy in reproducing LES-derived reaction rate fluctuations. Subsequently, the linearized governing equations, including the linearized EBU model for reaction rates, were solved for incoming acoustic perturbations. The resulting response modes indicate that reaction rate oscillations stem from Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings disturbing the jet flame. These findings align well with LES simulations regarding the mode shapes of both velocity and reaction rate fluctuations. Ultimately, the linear EBU model successfully captured reaction rate fluctuations that differed significantly from those in non-reacting flow, confirming its utility in analyzing reacting flows. This methodology offers a promising approach for investigating the flow response to acoustic actuation in practical, DNS-and-LES-inaccessible flows. However, the significant linear stability growth suggests that the underlying assumptions, such as the existence of a steady turbulent state, may break down, implying that the linear analysis results require verification through DNS or LES.

If this interaction violates lepton number, the $\Delta L=2$ transition is directly mediated by the dark matter field, bypassing the suppression typically caused by small neutrino masses, thereby producing a significant effect on decay rates. Because ultralight dark matter behaves as a classical field, the resulting decay events exhibit a periodic modulation. However, we observe that in the early Universe, such a coupling would likely disrupt standard cosmological models. Specifically, the necessity for neutrinos to free-stream prior to matter-radiation equality imposes strict constraints on the parameter space, rendering the detection of any signal in future $0\nu \beta\beta$ experiments extremely unlikely, even with meV-level sensitivity to the effective neutrino mass. To overcome these cosmological constraints, the dark matter must subsequently decouple from neutrinos; we examine two distinct decoupling mechanisms and their implications for the $\Delta L=2$ signal in $0\nu \beta\beta$ decay. First, we consider total decoupling, which eliminates the periodicity of the signal and restricts the scenario to a negligible contribution to the decay rate. Second, we propose utilizing axion domain walls as the source of periodicity instead. This approach relaxes the pre-decoupling constraints and allows the $\Delta L=2$ interaction to remain within reach of upcoming experiments, despite the eventual erasure of the axion domain walls.

, nonlocal extension of Einstein's gravitational theory, modeled after the analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics in media. Within this framework, historical dependence is introduced through a constitutive relation that utilizes a causal kernel, which must ultimately be derived from observational data. This paper aims to reformulate nonlocal gravity so that the nonlocal components of the constitutive relation directly link measurable quantities, mirroring the approach found in nonlocal electrodynamics. The derived constitutive relation aligns with a recent proposal by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl [25]. Utilizing this updated constitutive relation for NLG, it is demonstrated that de Sitter spacetime does not constitute a valid solution. Furthermore, when applying NLG to derive the Schwarzschild solution with mass $M$, the condition $T^{\rm ext}_0 = 0$ must be met, where $T^{\rm ext}_0$ is the time component of the external stress-energy tensor. Consequently, if an object possesses internal stresses or is surrounded by a medium (implying $T^{\rm ext}_0 \neq 0$), the nonlocal effects of GR-NLG will alter its shape and internal properties relative to its general relativity state. These findings regarding NLG are considered significant. However, the scenario under which the Schwarzschild spacetime emerges as a solution to the nonlocal field equations appears both contrived and unlikely. Consequently, transitioning from local to nonlocal gravity may necessitate revisions to the constitutive relation that currently exclude such a possibility. Ultimately, updating both the constitutive relation and the prior assumption regarding the absence of nonlocal effects in Schwarzschild spacetime remains essential for accurately assessing the feasibility of implementing nonlocal gravity. Keywords: nonlocal gravity, Schwarzschild spacetime, de Sitter spacetime, constitutive relation. PACS: 04.20.Fy, 95.30.Sg.

We present a statistical framework that leverages genome-wide association statistics to pinpoint classes of genomic elements that are either enriched for or depleted regarding loci influencing a specific trait, with the model inherently accommodating multiple annotation types. Applying this approach to GWAS data for 18 human traits—including red and platelet cell metrics, glucose and lipid levels, height, BMI, and Crohn's disease—we assessed the relevance of 450 genomic annotations across over a hundred tissues and cell lines, covering protein-coding genes, enhancers, and DNase-I hypersensitive sites. Our results indicate that the proportion of phenotype-associated SNPs affecting protein sequences varies by trait, ranging from approximately 2% for platelet volume to roughly 20% for LDL cholesterol. Additionally, we observed significant depletion of repressed chromatin for SNPs linked to several traits and enrichment of cell type-specific DNase-I hypersensitive sites for others (e.g., spleen-specific sites for platelet volume). Finally, re-weighting GWAS results using functional genomics data increased the count of high-confidence associated loci by approximately 5%. This study demonstrates a computational pipeline for integrating functional genomics data to assess the genomic distribution of GWAS-associated variants across diverse phenotypes and genomic landscapes, thereby revealing the distinct genomic architectures underlying diverse human traits.

Galactic Centre that have not exhibited outbursts over a ten-year monitoring period has led to the hypothesis of a substantial population of stellar-mass black holes in this area. A fundamental premise of this argument is the assertion that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries (LMXBs) do not experience long intervals between transients. However, this paper demonstrates that approximately half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade when observed with MAXI sensitivity. Furthermore, we show that to align the expected total number of neutron star LMXBs with both current observations and the galaxy's millisecond radio pulsar population, the dominant class of these systems must have recurrence times far surpassing a century for MAXI-detectable outbursts, implying that few such systems have been identified to date. We also discuss the implications of these findings for estimates of the total black hole mass within the Galactic Centre. Our conclusions rely solely on well-established facts regarding neutron star physics and observable quantities, avoiding any dependence on theoretical assumptions concerning accretion disk behavior. Consequently, the variable source in Sgr A0 is best explained as a infalling star around the primary black hole rather than a missed neutron star LMXB, and the total black hole mass in the Galactic Centre is more accurately estimated at 1040 $M_{\odot}$ ($^{+160}_{-100}$ $M_{\odot}$) instead of $620 \pm 50 \, M_{\odot}$.

Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control. Furthermore, these phenomena offer striking, verifiable predictions relevant to unexplained anomalies observed in certain high-$T_c$ superconductors. Using clearly defined, quantitative principles of shaking matter, researchers can retrospectively analyze existing data on unconventional superconductors and other complex materials, or proactively design experiments to test these predictions in new systems. Since Einstein's 1905 special relativity (SR) established that moving masses experience time dilation and length contraction, the century-old question arises whether these phenomena, or related effects like the Coriolis force, influence electrons in moving atoms or molecules. These outcomes align with, and can be understood through, the classical centrifugal field and redshift effects. Additionally, we demonstrate that perpendicular ion velocity generates a spin-rotation coupling, causing core electron spins to orient against the direction of motion (antiparallel). First, we introduce a new metric leveraging Natural Language Inference (NLI) to assess the semantic variety of a model's response set. Validated against an existing framework (Tevet and Berant, 2021), our findings strongly suggest that NLI Diversity aligns with semantic diversity; notably, the contradiction relation proves more effective than the neutral relation for this purpose, and integrating NLI models with semantic embeddings yields superior results. Including the NLI Diversity metric in our analysis reveals that current models frequently generate repetitive responses. Specifically, T0-30B tends to reuse subsets of completed samples, whereas Facebook AI/LLaMA models display more varied semantic content across different inputs. Overall, our experiments demonstrate that MLB loss functions effectively replace cross entropy loss, and the direct training of MLB-trained models on test data confirms the feasibility of this approach. We have numerically modeled these rotating objects to determine whether they can sustain nuclear fusion as their energy source, accounting for significant rotational deformation rather than assuming slow rotation. For various angular momentum values, we derived critical curves in the mass versus central degeneracy parameter space where nuclear energy generation equals surface luminosity. Our results indicate that when angular momentum surpasses a threshold of $J_0=8.85\times 10^{48}{\rm erg}~{\rm s}$, the critical curve splits into two branches representing lower and higher degeneracy due to the mass-shedding limit. Based on these findings, we simulated the mechano-thermal evolution of substellar objects under two simplified scenarios involving cooling and reductions in mass or angular momentum. In the first scenario, dominated by external braking mechanisms like magnetized winds or magnetic braking, the evolution is primarily governed by the spin-down timescale. In the second scenario, lacking external braking, gravitational contraction drives the object to the mass-shedding limit, after which it ejects mass to form a surrounding ring or disc and subsequently shrinks. Our findings suggest that an isolated brown dwarf with mass $M=0.08~\rm M_\odot$ and initial conditions matching the second scenario would eject mass at a rate of $\dot{J}\sim 2\times 10^{-10}~\rm M_\odot$ to reach the mass-shedding limit within approximately $10^8$ years. These outcomes are based on simplified physical assumptions; consequently, we anticipate that incorporating more detailed physics, such as molecular formation, ionization, opacities, and relativistic effects, will cause the critical curves and evolutionary timescales to shift from our current estimates. Our proposed simple models can serve as foundational elements for more advanced simulations of rotating brown dwarfs.

These structures are frequently depicted in a two-tiered layout, where each entity set is shown as a collection of vertices aligned on one of two parallel horizontal lines, and their relationships are illustrated by edges linking corresponding vertices across the lines. A primary goal in creating such visualizations is to reduce edge crossings; however, minimizing crossings is computationally demanding and often yields drawings with so many intersections that they compromise readability. This work examines a recent method for eliminating crossings by splitting vertices, aiming to identify the minimum number of vertices that must be split to achieve a planar representation. We demonstrate that deciding whether a planar drawing is achievable by splitting at most $k$ vertices is fixed parameter tractable with respect to $k$. Furthermore, we show that this problem is also fixed parameter tractable when parameterized by the genus of the surface on which the drawing is planned to be planar. Additionally, we address the problem of finding a near-optimal solution within constant factors, and we establish lower bounds for these problems when the genus is zero. Regarding bipartite graphs that are already planar, we prove that at most $n$ vertices need to be split to maintain planarity, addressing a query raised by Angelini et al. (2018). For general bipartite graphs, we provide an upper bound of $5n+O(\sqrt{n})$. We also explore related problems for graphs embedded in surfaces of genus $g$, offering improved bounds for graphs with low genus and generalizing results from Angelini et al. (2018) regarding planar drawings via vertex splitting. Finally, we present explicit constructions that validate these bounds up to additive terms, and throughout the paper, we include detailed analyses and calculations of specific examples.

approach enabling multiple parties to collaboratively train robust machine learning models without exchanging their sensitive data. Based on collaboration structures, FL is categorized into Horizontal Federated Learning (HFL) and Vertical Federated Learning (VFL). In HFL, entities share identical feature spaces and data samples, whereas in VFL, they share common sample identifiers and collaborate on features. VFL offers a wider application scope and is particularly well-suited for joint model training among large enterprises.

This paper concentrates on VFL, examining potential privacy vulnerabilities within real-world frameworks. We developed and executed two practical privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical analysis demonstrates that these attacks are (1) effective, allowing adversaries to extract private training data even when intermediate outputs are encrypted; (2) evasive, as they adhere strictly to protocol specifications and do not degrade the target model's accuracy; and (3) low-effort, requiring minimal prior knowledge of the target participant's data distribution. Furthermore, we show that the information leaked is as potent as the original training data for training alternative classifiers. Finally, we discuss potential countermeasures and their associated challenges, aiming to inspire future research directions.

numerous machine learning challenges; however, their reliance on pairwise evaluations causes computational complexity to rise with data volume, limiting their utility on large-scale datasets. To overcome this, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, enabling scalability. Despite its popularity, RFF has notable limitations: because it samples features from a distribution independent of the training data, it demands a large number of feature dimensions to match the performance of kernelized classifiers, a requirement that scales with dataset size. Consequently, reducing feature dimensions is essential for effective scaling. This paper introduces Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), a data-dependent kernel approximation technique designed to minimize feature dimensions and enhance predictive performance. The method is evaluated on classification and regression tasks, with comparisons made against RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach. Experimental results show that PRFF requires significantly fewer feature dimensions than RFF to achieve comparable performance. Additionally, the study offers a theoretical analysis of the gap between PRFF and the original kernel classifier. Finally, both synthetic and real-world experiments are presented to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. Traditional methods for assessing attack effectiveness typically rely on macro-level metrics, like the critical percolation probability ($p_c$) and the size of the giant component, often overlooking the micro-level dynamics of node removals, their specific traits, and immediate outcomes. This paper introduces and applies a micro-scale approach to attack analysis. Grounded in network percolation theory, we examine the "avalanche" effect triggered by the removal of a single node from the giant component—a phenomenon where one removal causes a cascade of disconnections that significantly contributes to network fragmentation and immunization beyond the loss of that single node. We specifically analyze the avalanche size, defined as the count of nodes disconnected from the giant component due to one removal. Furthermore, regarding random attacks on Cayley tree networks, we analytically derive the distribution of avalanche sizes throughout the entire attack process, from initiation until the network is fully dismantled and the attack ceases. Our findings reveal that avalanche sizes follow a uniform distribution. Additionally, we demonstrate that the average avalanche size surpasses the initial removal degree, indicating that an attack's true destructive power exceeds that of the targeted node alone. These results offer a more nuanced and comprehensive evaluation of random attack efficacy and are broadly applicable to the study of network attacks and immunization.

Deep learning has achieved success in various fields, including image processing, natural language understanding, and biomedical analysis. However, the heavy computational costs of these models often hinder their deployment on edge devices with limited processing power, such as smartphones, tablets, and wearables. To address this, models must be compressed through pruning, knowledge distillation, and quantization. This paper reviews state-of-the-art model compression techniques, classifies them, and offers insights for developers. We present an extended version of a previously introduced survey on model compression, featuring a comprehensive evaluation of state-of-the-art methods. By analyzing the strengths and limitations of each approach, we derive key insights and propose future research directions. Our findings highlight an increasing trend in end-to-end network compression, a rise in occlusion- and pose-aware face reconstruction studies, and the growing use of lightweight models with attention mechanisms and self-supervised learning for specific tasks like head pose estimation and face alignment. Additionally, we discuss the limitations of current research and suggest potential directions for future work. The source code for this survey is available at https://github.com/ManjuRajamani/Deep-Learning-Face-Compression-Survey.

Although this phenomenon is often blamed on forecasting inaccuracies or operational breakdowns, we argue it stems from risk-averse scheduling strategies. By applying a stochastic self-scheduling model to real-world data from the Australian National Electricity Market, we show that risk-averse storage units adopt a short-sighted operational approach. Specifically, they focus primarily on near-term price arbitrage, targeting only a limited number of extreme price peaks and valleys, which leaves them inactive during many periods characterized by significantly high or low prices. These findings suggest risks-aversion serves as an underappreciated factor contributing to inadequate storage response to price signals and advise regulators to value storage capabilities based on their willingness to operate during scarcity and surplus conditions, rather than solely on forecasted MWh or kW metrics. The proposed stochastic framework offers a useful tool for assessing the operational behavior of storage units with various risk preferences.

The model incorporates simplified linear boundary layer friction, Newtonian cooling, and dry convective adjustment. Through a series of controlled experiments, researchers varied the planetary rotation rate and the imposed equator-to-pole temperature gradient. These variables were converted into dimensionless parameters to define a parameter space where distinct circulation regimes are identified and categorized. Significant trends emerge when altering the planetary rotation rate alongside frictional and thermal relaxation timescales. The progression of circulation regimes with respect to planetary rotation closely mirrors findings from laboratory studies on rotating, stratified fluids, particularly when topographic $\beta$-effects are included to simulate planetary vorticity gradients caused by spherical curvature. Additionally, a regular baroclinic wave regime appears at intermediate thermal Rossby numbers, with its characteristics and dominant zonal wavenumber heavily influenced by radiative and frictional damping strengths. These regular waves display notable similarities to baroclinic storms observed on Mars under specific conditions. At the highest rotation rates, multiple jets develop when the Rossby deformation radius and other eddy-related scales are significantly smaller than the planetary radius; these resemble the multiple zonal jets found on gas giant planets. These jets form on scales comparable to the most energetic eddies, poleward of the supercritical latitude, near the Rhines scale. Finally, the balance of forces within these multiple jets is examined by analyzing the time- and depth-mean zonal momentum equation. The study concludes by outlining the limitations imposed by the use of a simplified GCM. These results enhance our comprehension of the fundamental physics and mechanism driving multiple jet formation on rapidly rotating planets with an atmosphere, an process also relevant to the multiple jets observed on Saturn, Jupiter, and Neptune. Notably, this includes the jets on Mars's southern hemisphere, which, while located at higher latitudes than on other terrestrial planets, can be explained by their scale being similar to the Rossby deformation radius.

The recent achievements of self-supervised pretraining (SSP) underscore the significance of leveraging vast amounts of unlabeled data to improve model outcomes. In this study, we investigate the combination of AL and SSP using ImageNet. We observe that performance on small toy datasets—the standard benchmark in current literature—does not accurately reflect performance on ImageNet, as active learners tend to select class-imbalanced samples. Among the existing baselines tested, popular AL algorithms across various small and large-scale settings fail to surpass random sampling. To address the issue of class imbalance, we introduce Balanced Selection (BASE), a straightforward and scalable AL algorithm that consistently outperforms random sampling by choosing more balanced samples for annotation compared to current methods. Our code is available at: https://github.com/zeyademam/active_learning.

Our findings indicate that conventional AL algorithms are underperforming because the metrics used for small-scale evaluations are inappropriate for image classification tasks like ImageNet. Furthermore, we show that a simple algorithm such as BASE can yield significant results. We anticipate these insights will guide future research.

In this study, we develop a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method within the positive-P phase-space framework specifically for interacting Bose gases. This approach surpasses current hydrodynamic models, including superfluid and generalized hydrodynamics, by enabling the simulation of complete quantum dynamics; it can calculate non-equilibrium quantum correlations, even at short wavelengths. Based on this framework, we formulate a linearized stochastic hydrodynamic scheme that extends the simulation duration for non-equilibrium scenarios beyond the limits of the full positive-P method, though this involves approximating quantum fluctuations. We demonstrate that this linearized scheme aligns directly with established Bogoliubov methods. Additionally, we validate the utility and benefits of this formalism by investigating correlations in a quantum shock wave scenario and contrasting its predictions with other standard quantum many-body approaches. Furthermore, this work delineates the criteria under which such quantum correlations can be derived and calculated using quantum hydrodynamic methods. The presented formalism and its applications are transferable to other systems, as they rely solely on fundamental quantum many-body principles. Ultimately, this method represents a significant advancement toward determining quantum correlations in the context of interacting Bose gases.

In the context of the annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of these words, the rate function corresponds to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of words. Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander \cite{BGdH10} established the quenched LDP (conditional on a typical letter sequence) for scenarios where renewal times exhibit an algebraic tail; their derived rate function consists of two components: the annealed rate function and a second term proportional to the specific relative entropy between the observed and reference laws of letters, where the reference law is generated by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This proportionality constant matches the tail exponent of the renewal process. The current paper aims to generalize both LDPs to cases where the underlying letter sequences are not i.i.d. It demonstrates that both principles remain valid when the letter sequence satisfies a mixing condition known as \emph{summable variation}. The resulting rate functions are still expressed as specific relative entropies with respect to the reference laws of words and letters, respectively. However, because neither reference law is i.i.d., the extension requires several approximation arguments. A key finding is that the independence of words in the induced process depends directly on the independence of the renewal times; consequently, the non-equilibrium nature of this word process arises from both the lack of independence in renewal times and the initial condition of the first word. This non-equilibrium character is captured by two additional terms in the quenched rate function: one reflecting the lack of independence in renewal times and the other reflecting the lack of independence in the initial condition. A grid search was employed to determine optimal reconstruction parameters for low-resolution 4D-MRI, specifically spatial resolution and temporal regularization. (NASDAQ) validates the generalizability of this approach for predicting other corporate stocks, including cryptocurrencies and global stock markets. There is a well-established history of analyzing and creating structure-preserving discretization methods, ranging from proving that standard schemes retain these properties to designing novel high-order schemes that exactly preserve them. However, when combined with implicit time-stepping, a significant drawback is that these properties typically depend on solving the potentially nonlinear systems of equations exactly at each time step. We illustrate its effectiveness by applying it to both conservation law systems and dissipative systems. FGMRES with constraints (FGC) is increasingly relevant for the evolving field of machine learning, where solving nonlinear systems is a key step in many popular methods, such as solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) for distributions within Hamiltonian or Neural ODEs. We hope this work provides a straightforward yet potent tool to enhance the accuracy of machine learning algorithms that solve PDEs. Furthermore, the proposed FGC method is universally applicable to any nonlinear system solver that can iterate linearly, including the authenticator technique. Beyond its immediate applications, this approach may serve as a straightforward mechanism to incorporate constraints into other numerical methods.

However, the massive computational and energy demands required for training and deploying ANNs have historically hindered their large-scale implementation. Concurrently, neuromorphic computing platforms have emerged as a promising alternative, successfully executing bio-realistic Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) with high throughput and minimal power usage. This paper proposes the Random Neural Network (RNN)—a spiking neural network with significant theoretical and practical advantages—as a versatile classifier capable of matching ANN performance on various tasks while leveraging the efficiency of SNNs. The efficacy of this approach is validated through experiments on multiple real-world classification datasets. Notably, the results demonstrate that the RNN achieves within a 1% gap of ANN performance while utilizing a model complexity roughly 20 times smaller, all while operating with the full efficiency of an SNN. Furthermore, the paper outlines the necessary training algorithms and provides computational evidence that the RNN avoids both overfitting and label leakage. Finally, it is emphasized that this work represents the first demonstration of the RNN's capability to solve the DNA base pairing task, a challenge that has previously eluded other SNN classifiers. Collectively, these findings indicate that the random neural network is a highly effective "off-the-shelf" classifier for diverse tasks, ranging from fundamental scientific problems to complex, real-world applications. The implications of this research are profound, warranting further investigation into optimal configuration and training strategies for even greater efficiency. This work utilizes the WNS1 chip from WinSemi, Israel, and features accompanying code available at https://github.com/mohamedameda/RNN.

Since its introduction, the RNN has garnered substantial attention and repeatedly proven successful at solving a wide array of tasks, from basic scientific challenges to intricate real-world problems.
