Originating in the 1970s through the work of Las Vergnas and Häggkvist, the investigation of graphs with the PMH-property integrates three fundamental graph concepts: matchings, Hamiltonicity, and edge-colourings. This study focuses on cubic graphs, aiming to characterize those where every perfect matching aligns with a specific colour in a proper 3-edge-colouring. We demonstrate that this condition is equivalent to the graphs being even-2-factorable (E2F), meaning all their 2-factors consist exclusively of even cycles. While bipartite cubic graphs trivially satisfy the E2F property, our analysis is restricted to non-bipartite cubic graphs. Although the PMH-property provides a sufficient (though not necessary) condition for a cubic graph to be E2F, the primary objective of this work is to define an infinite family of non-bipartite, E2F cubic graphs parameterized by two variables, which we term "papillon graphs." We further determine the specific parameter values under which these papillon graphs exhibit the PMH-property or are merely E2F, also calculating the exact count of edges that must be removed to render the graph E2F for other parameter combinations. Additionally, we establish that papillon graphs are Hamiltonian, and under certain conditions, they contain a perfect matching composed entirely of non-bridge edges. The title of this article honors the French term for papillon graphs, reflecting the butterfly shape observed in the 2-factors of these structures. Papillon graphs generalize various existing cubic graphs; however, unlike papillon graphs, most other cubic graphs are not E2F. Our findings indicate that a significant subset of papillon graphs possess the PMH-property, whereas the remainder are still capable of being made 2-factorable by removing two edges. The term "papillon graph" was introduced to distinguish this construction from the "papillon graph family" described by Albert and Alexander (2014). This research extends the work of Oliveira and Sampaio (2018) by exploring the conditions under which papillon graphs have the PMH-property or are E2F, and it contrasts with the results of Van den Heuvel (2001), which characterized E2F cubic graphs via the PMH-property and the existence of a specific

for automatically generating system call filtering policies tailored to containerized microservices. During runtime, Timeloops identifies which system calls a program should execute while blocking unauthorized attempts. It overcomes several limitations of current static analysis approaches, particularly in creating precise filters for interpreted languages like Python, PHP, and JavaScript. The system relies on a straightforward and robust architecture built from established, off-the-shelf technologies—including seccomp-BPF, systemd, and Podman containers—requiring fewer than 500 lines of code. We validate Timeloops by learning system call behaviors for individual services and two microservice benchmarks utilizing popular frameworks such as Python Flask, Nginx (with PHP and Lua), Apache Thrift, and databases like Redis, Memcached, and MongoDB. Additionally, Timeloops achieves performance comparable to an unhardened system on an amortized basis while producing more compact system call filters than existing static analysis methods. Finally, the system is available open-source at https://github.com/andrewseng/Timeloops.

This study introduces a novel state representation for soccer combined with batch reinforcement learning to train a policy network capable of determining the best action. Wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) alleviates the requirement for strict adherence to the physical wave equation during iterations, whereas extended source waveform inversion (ESI) employs a non-physical source distributed across the computational domain that iteratively migrates toward the true physical source. Both WRI and ESI operate within a shared mathematical framework utilizing the Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method, with a specific emphasis on time-domain formulations using extended sources. Conceptually, WRI and ESI can be regarded as weighted variants of classical FWI. To efficiently solve the resulting normal equations in a matrix-free manner, the conjugate gradient method is applied, leveraging the symmetric positive definite Hessian; this approach supports both time and frequency domain wave equation solvers. However, the primary challenge remains the substantial storage requirements needed to retain time-domain wavefields throughout the iterative process. To address this, two strategies are proposed: extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data directly instead of wavefields. It is recommended that these approaches be further investigated to develop more tractable workflows. Additionally, this methodology can be adapted to solve other prominent imaging equations. To validate these findings, extensive numerical tests are required to compare the methods while varying key parameters, specifically the extent of source coverage, the distance between the extended and physical sources, and the sampling interval of the time-domain data. Ultimately, applying these advanced techniques to real datasets remains a critical future step.

immigration and a competition-dispersal tradeoff jointly influence the dynamics of two species competing for space on regular lattices. In this system, one species can invade only nearest-neighbor sites, whereas the other species can invade sites at any distance but possesses lower local competitiveness, establishing with a probability $g \le 1$. Immigration is incorporated as external noise that spontaneously replaces an individual at a lattice site with one from the opposing species. This interplay of mechanisms generates diverse competitive outcomes, ranging from the exclusion of one species to mono-stable coexistence at fixed population ratios, as well as bi-stable coexistence where population proportions depend on initial conditions. Notably, within the bi-stable regime, increasing immigration intensity beyond a critical threshold triggers a discontinuous transition. This results in a "half loop" dynamics characteristic of a cusp catastrophe, ultimately causing the irreversible extinction of the species with the limited dispersal range. This extinction threshold is lower than that in a symmetric species interaction model, indicating that high immigration can more effectively induce the "competitive exclusion" of a slow disperser when interspecific competition is stronger than intraspecific competition. Furthermore, the model exhibits a second critical point where an unstable fixed point emerges from a node, giving rise to a pair of bi-stable fixed points as immigration continues to increase. These two points annihilate each other at a second cusp, after which an unstable fixed point appears and monostable bi-stable coexistence ensues. Finally, all fixed points disappear at a limit point, leading to chaotic dynamics marked by a self-organized critical state of complete extinction for one species. This extinction threshold is highest within the bi-stable region; however, it is still lower than the threshold required for the irreversible "competitive exclusion" of the slow disperser. We observe that this complete extinction also forms a half loop when iterating over the lattice size, with the apex located at parameters identical to those of the irreversible competitive exclusion. Our findings demonstrate that the noisy voter model successfully captures the complexity of interface growth in the bi-stable regime and the full range of extinction mechanisms, including complete extinction akin to the "competitive exclusion" principle. These results are consistent with established mean field models of noisy voter dynamics and the Bramson-Tamari process.

which integrates data and energy networks with device-to-device (D2D) communication coexistence. In this architecture, a base station (BS) delivers data to information-requiring users (IUs) and energy to energy-requiring users (EUs) via a time-fraction-based information and energy transfer (TFIET) scheme. Additionally, the system permits D2D communications to share the spectrum with the BS, thereby addressing the escalating demands for energy and spectrum in next-generation networks. However, interference from D2D links and wireless propagation losses can substantially reduce IU data throughput. To mitigate these challenges, we propose integrating an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) into the DED2D framework. Consequently, we formulate an optimization problem designed to jointly optimize the information and energy beamformers for IUs and EUs, the TFIET time fractions, D2D transmit powers, and IRS reflection coefficients. The objective is to maximize the minimum throughput of IUs while ensuring that EUs meet their harvested energy requirements and D2D users satisfy their rate thresholds. Since the resulting max-min throughput problem is computationally intractable, we develop an alternating descent algorithm to solve it efficiently with low complexity. Simulation results validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. Contributions of this work include: (a) a comprehensive analysis of the interference landscape within the DED2D system and a demonstration of how an IRS can significantly enhance IU throughput, and (b) an efficient low-complexity solution to a high-dimensional optimization problem that jointly optimizes multiple vectors and scalars to solve a max-min throughput issue. Keywords: energy harvesting, IRS, DED2D, base station, information and energy beamformer, TFIET, max-min throughput.

This project details the technical creation of a two-dimensional (2D) Laser Doppler Vibrometry (LDV) measurement utilizing a single-point LDV system via an automated, remote-controlled workflow. The goal of this report is to facilitate the rapid deployment of setups for comparable applications. Additionally, the described configuration is modular and has been employed to evaluate the modal response of samples excited by both air-based acoustic signals and mechanical induction. Crucially, this arrangement requires only one camera, making it adaptable to high-speed environments through the integration of polarization beam splitters and a splitter/combinator lens system. While this report focuses on excitation methods based on air acoustics and mechanical induction, the described arrangement can be extended to include other high-frequency excitation techniques, such as laser-induced forward transfer or ultrasound transducers. This, in turn, would enable the acquisition of data through multiple excitations within a brief timeframe. Ultimately, the proposed system offers a versatile solution for experimentalists conducting various air-acoustic, mechanical, and high-frequency laser excitations, allowing for multiple response measurements in a short period without discarding data. By comparing the proposed method against current state-of-the-art solutions, it is demonstrated that this approach effectively accomplishes all necessary tasks for a standard LDV experiment with high efficiency, low cost, and significant adaptability.

This study examines various designs aimed specifically at mitigating spherical aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEM). Through numerical analysis, we assess the potential of these phase plates to achieve spatial resolutions as fine as 1 Ångström on standard, uncorrected TEM systems. Additionally, we present a comprehensive analysis of the spectrum resulting from the linearization around these solitary waves. Our results indicate that no instability arises from $\mathbf{R}$-solitary waves; specifically, the linearized operator's spectrum contains no negative values. Furthermore, we prove that any unstable mode must be oscillatory and that the index is even. For orbital stability, we establish sufficient conditions based on the convexity of the embedding. These findings align with previous observations made for the nonlinear Schr\"odinger equation. The paper also includes a detailed examination of the linearized operator's behavior at infinity.

Specifically, for a Galois extension K/Q where the Galois group G is isomorphic to A4, S4, or A5, we provide necessary and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers of K to be free over its corresponding order within the rational group algebra Q[G]. This study examines the complementary nature of these signatures for the Belle II experiment, specifically focusing on axion-like particles ($a$) generated from meson decays. We introduce a novel approach to detect two-body decays characterized by $B^+ \to K^+ a$ followed by $a\to E\!\!\!/$, where $E\!\!\!/$ represents missing energy. Utilizing an integrated luminosity of $50\,$ab$^{-1}$, Belle II is capable of probing light invisible resonances with branching ratios $\mathcal{B}(B^+\to K^+ a) \gtrsim 10^{-7}$ and decay lengths $c\tau_a \gtrsim 1\,$m. For axion-like particles, we anticipate that the sensitivity of the $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ channel to small couplings could improve by up to two orders of magnitude relative to prior searches at fixed-target and collider facilities. Specifically, for sub-GeV particles, the combination of $B^+ \to K^+ E\!\!\!/$ at Belle II and beam-dump experiments offers the greatest sensitivity, whereas for heavier particles, the smallest couplings can be probed through the detection of scattered $K^+$ mesons. Consequently, the future program at Belle II will significantly constrain the parameter space of long-lived axion-like particles. This analysis also holds relevance for other neutral LLPs, including dark photons, sterile neutrinos, and scalar particles. The proposed strategy can be readily adapted to investigate neutral LLPs arising from non-$B$-factory processes, such as proton-proton interactions. Furthermore, we detail the characteristics of the Belle II dataset favorable for this search, outline the required analysis techniques, and present simple estimates of sensitivity for specific model examples. The code implementing these estimates is accessible on GitHub. While the discussion centers on Belle II, the underlying approach is broadly applicable to any collider featuring a high-$\beta^*$ configuration. This method represents a significant advancement over previous studies, which were limited to short decay lengths ($c\tau_a \lesssim 10\,$m) and relied on the assumption of approximately isotropic LLP production.

We first introduce an ensemble method that surpasses prior contextualized approaches, which then serves as the foundation for a detailed analysis of predicted semantic shifts in English vocabulary over five decades. Our results indicate that these methods frequently assign high change scores to words that are not actually undergoing genuine diachronic semantic shifts, or where the validity of such shifts is dubious. We provide detailed discussions of these challenging instances with specific examples and propose corresponding linguistic classifications. Ultimately, we conclude that pre-trained contextualized language models tend to conflate changes in lexicographic senses with variations in contextual frequency, a bias inherent to their distributional nature that differs from issues seen in static embedding methods. Furthermore, these models often blend syntactic and semantic features of lexical items. Finally, we suggest several potential future solutions to address these problems. To ensure the reliable detection of authentic diachronic semantic shifts in lexical semantics research, researchers must carefully consider the limitations of automated, corpus-based, in silico experiments. This requires either the development of specialized tools tailored to diachronic analysis or the rigorous validation of findings against historical dictionaries and other diachronic semantic data sources. Our case studies and proposals are grounded in first-principles linguistic reasoning, demonstrating that such expertise is essential for correctly interpreting diachronic semantic variations in lexical items. This applies not only to specific case instances but also to the broader categories of errors exhibited by these models.

movement of nuclei between the apical and basal surfaces of the neuroepithelium, known as interkinetic nuclear migration (IKNM). In this study, we utilize long-term, rapid lightsheet and two-photon imaging of zebrafish retinas *in vivo* during early development to identify the physical mechanisms driving nuclear behavior during IKNM. These imaging techniques enable the reliable tracking of nuclear movements and divisions within densely packed populations during early retinogenesis. By analyzing these tracks, we formulate and validate a theoretical model of retinal IKNM as a diffusive process influenced by a nuclear concentration gradient established by the continuous addition of new nuclei at the apical surface. Our findings elucidate how apical nuclear packing affects migration dynamics, offer a robust quantitative account of nuclear distribution across the retina, and suggest potential implications for stochastic cell fate decisions in this system. Overall, this work provides a quantitative foundation for investigating the biophysical drivers of coordinated cell fate acquisition in developing tissues.

In these contexts, physically viable code patterns are inherently non-negative, systematically structured, and often lack the incoherence properties found in other patterns like Gaussian codes, which can hinder reconstruction quality. This paper addresses this by designing code patterns for video compressed sensing and demosaicing that minimize the mutual coherence of the matrix $\boldsymbol{\Phi\Psi}$, where $\boldsymbol{\Phi}$ is the sensing matrix derived from the code and $\boldsymbol{\Psi}$ represents the signal basis. Our primary contribution lies in explicitly incorporating the specific structural constraints required by these applications: (1) non-negativity, (2) block-diagonal structure, and (3) circular shifting. Notably, the circular shifting property facilitates accurate and seamless patch-wise reconstruction within certain compressed sensing frameworks. To achieve this, we employ an evolutionary algorithm, specifically a genetic algorithm, to optimize the parameters within the circular shifting operation. We validate the efficacy of the proposed codes through numerical experiments on both synthetic data and real-world data, covering single-frame and multi-frame reconstruction of compressed measurements in video compressed sensing and static image demosaicing. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of these codes in video compressed sensing and real-time sensor fusion for mosaic imaging. The resulting optimized codes are readily deployable in video compressed sensing; however, as current sensors are incompatible with circular shifting, our codes are specifically designed for real-time sensor fusion using algorithms like those in reference [1], which is why the reconstruction images in our experiments were generated via this method. Our codes are available for download at https://sites.google.com/view/vid-sense/codes.

Our theory demonstrates that these fluids can maintain coherent motion, characterized by a non-zero mean velocity in the hydrodynamic limit, despite the disruptive effects of the disorder. Nevertheless, linearized hydrodynamics fails to capture the scaling behavior of these active systems in spatial dimensions ranging from 2 to 5. Amidst rising fraud in the current era, verification processes utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Natural Language Processing (NLP) for ID card extraction have been implemented to prevent account fraud. OCR technology converts images into text, enabling the extraction of data from Indonesian identity cards (KTP) to facilitate easier data entry for service operators. Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack (YORP) effect, a net torque generated by the reflection and thermal re-emission of solar radiation from their surfaces. This phenomenon causes a gradual alteration in rotation periods, which is most readily observable in light curves due to the quadratic accumulation of phase shifts over time. We gathered archived light curves and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids (10115) 1992 SK, (1620) Geographos, and (1685) Toro. Using light curve inversion, we fitted the data to convex shape models, modeling the YORP effect as a linear variation in rotation frequency ($\upsilon \equiv \mathrm{d}\omega / \mathrm{d}t$) and optimizing it alongside other spin and shape parameters. For asteroid (10115) 1992 SK, we detected a rotational acceleration of $\upsilon = (8.3 \pm 0.6) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, which aligns well with theoretical predictions for its specific shape and spin model. Regarding (1685) Toro, we measured $\upsilon = (3.3 \pm 0.3) \times 10^{-9}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$, representing a lower limit as the object was observed near eastern elongation. For (1620) Geographos, our initial estimate was $\upsilon = (-1.0 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$; however, incorporating a model of the surface Phoenicam crater as a dark region reduced the magnitude to $\upsilon = (-6.3 \pm 0.9) \times 10^{-8}\,\mathrm{rad}\,\mathrm{d}^{-2}$. This value falls within the range of previous estimates derived from light curve analyses, which spanned from negative to positive. The new YORP measurement for (1685) Toro is the first quantitative result, and both findings for (10115) 1992 SK and (1620) Geographos align with current theoretical models.

group of a compact surface, which fixes the boundary and acts with sufficient transitivity on the interior, can be Roelcke precompact when equipped with the topology inherited from the compact-open topology. Consequently, no subgroup of this group can serve as the topological uniformity of a countable uniform space. This second result follows from the observation that the compact-open topology is an initial topology derived from continuous mappings into a compact space. However, this topology is not the fine uniformity of the same topology; specifically, the identity map from the space under the compact-open topology to it equipped with the fine uniformity is not uniformly continuous. We illustrate these findings using various topologies defined on countable sets, including those arising from the rational numbers, ordered countable ordinal numbers, and the one-point compactification of such spaces. Furthermore, we examine the scenario where the boundary is not fixed. Ultimately, this work aims to clarify the distinctions among the compact-open, box (or uniform), and order topologies (when applicable) on the rational numbers and on countable ordinal spaces.

equivalently defined by MSO-transducers, streaming $\omega$-string transducers, or deterministic two-way transducers with look-ahead. When restricted to the one-way model, these transducers characterize rational functions. Despite the robust characterization of regular functions by various finite-state devices, even the subclass of rational functions may include functions that are not computable by a Turing machine with infinite input. This paper introduces a decision procedure for the synthesis problem: given a regular function $f$ (specified by one of the aforementioned transducer models), determine if $f$ is computable, and if so, construct a Turing machine that computes it. For regular functions, we demonstrate that computability is equivalent to continuity, thereby reducing the problem to deciding continuity. We provide a generic characterization of continuity for functions that preserve regular languages under inverse image, such as regular functions, and utilize this to prove the decidability of continuity (and consequently computability) for both rational and regular functions. For rational functions, we show that this decision can be made in $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$ (previously established as $\mathsf{PTime}$ by Prieur). Similarly, we effectively characterize the uniform continuity of regular functions and connect it to the concept of uniform computability, which provides stronger efficiency assurances. Our results extend to regular tree-to-tree functions, yielding the following contributions: we define regular functions as those recognizing regular languages under inverse image (aligning with the work of Karimov and Steifelt), prove their computability is decidable (contrast with infinite non-computable examples from \cite{DBLP:conf/lics/Zetzsche19}), decide the computability of such functions, and characterize their uniform continuity. To achieve this, we employ characterizations by streaming and two-way transducers with look-ahead for both rational and regular functions. Furthermore, our decision procedures are optimal regarding complexity for regular functions and improve upon previous best complexities for rational functions.

for variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) formulations—which yield the most permissive controller for state- and input-constrained problems subject to worst-case disturbances—we propose a second-order successive sweep algorithm to compute the zero sublevel sets of a standard reachability value functional. Assuming sufficient regularity and continuity of the HJI partial differential equation across the state space, we demonstrate that, under state feedback control against worst-case disturbances, this method enables the computation of the reachable state set within a specified verification time horizon. Consequently, we derive conditions of uniform scalability for this approach within a fixed verification timeframe, noting that the state space can be increased indefinitely without impacting the algorithm's computational demand per step. Finally, validating these claims within the context of state-feedback optimal control, our numerical results indicate that this method can solve the standard nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) equation over the nonnegative real numbers in approximately one second. These findings are also applicable to state-dependent Riccati differential equations when the state dimension is one. While the requirement for the HJI equation to be uniformly Lipschitz continuous within the state space is somewhat restrictive, we show that this condition can be relaxed when solving for the reachable state set within a defined verification horizon. Although the method is Eulerian in nature and typically applicable only to state-HJ or parameterized state-HJ equations where the equation is solvable within a periodic domain, we confirm that it is generally applicable to any state-HJ problem aimed at determining the reachable state set within a specified verification time. Furthermore, unlike previous methods, our approach avoids spatial discretization of the state-HJ equation; instead, it relies solely on the time derivative of the verification-time-dependent target set, making it advantageous when high-fidelity solutions are required inside the reachable state set. We conclude by contrasting our technique with successive over-relaxation, successive constraint relaxation, and grid-based successive over-relaxation methods. Beyond its utility in computing the reachable state set, this technique can also be leveraged to calculate a lower bound of uniqueness for a said time-horizon-restricted reachable state set.

While the visual categorization hypothesis attributes this continuum to the presence of animal-diagnostic features, the agency hypothesis suggests it reflects the perception of animals as social agents. In this study, we tested both theories using a stimulus set where visual categorizability and agency were dissociated, based on convolutional neural network representations and behavioral data. fMRI results revealed that visual categorizability and agency account for independent components of the animacy continuum in VTC; when modeled together, they fully explain the continuum. Specifically, when reasoning about pairs of programs, this logic enables quantitative analysis of the degree to which pre- and postconditions regarding the relationship between program inputs and outputs are satisfied. To our knowledge, this marks the first quantitative generalization of the relational Hoare logic. In a similar vein to its predecessor, we establish soundness for this variant within a formal semantic framework grounded in operational semantics. Our soundness proof relies on utilizing superpositions of computational branches, a technique previously employed by Unruh (2019) for its relational counterpart. As in the standard relational Hoare logic, we address program misbehavior rather than errors. However, unlike the traditional single-threshold approach, our method employs a second, higher threshold to distinguish genuine errors from behaviors that merely exceed a level of correctness deemed acceptable for certain contexts. This approach was necessitated because, in quantum computing, achieving a postcondition with 100% probability is often unattainable or unnecessary; for instance, a postcondition satisfying the measurement outcomes with approximately 99.7% probability aligns with the three-sigma principle in statistical analysis.

This study examines a discrete-time, discrete-space, stochastic epidemic on a one-dimensional lattice, considering an infection with a fixed, general, irreducible, and positive diagonal infection probability matrix. We derive the asymptotic behavior of the total infected population size under the conditional event of extinction as population density approaches infinity. Furthermore, we introduce a novel component of this conditional extinction process termed the "environment after extinction," which characterizes the spatial distribution of individuals post-extinction. Our primary finding demonstrates that if the infection probability matrix is primitive, the environment after extinction converges exponentially fast to a non-degenerate random variable proportional to the left eigenvector of the infection probability matrix associated with the eigenvalue one. These results are particularly significant when the infection probability matrix exhibits a clustering structure, such as in the self-organized or periodic cases, where a non-degenerate limiting "environment after extinction" exists only conditionally on extinction and conditioned on the number of infected clusters. Additionally, we explore the implications of this characterization for the optimal control of the spatial distribution of infected individuals. To support these conclusions, extensive numerical simulations are presented. The primary contribution lies in establishing the convergence to a non-degenerate "environment after extinction" at an exponential rate, thereby generalizing previous results by Durett, Peierls, and Lynees. Earlier research has also highlighted the importance of super-spreader events in accelerating epidemic transmission; for instance, in a related model without spatial structure, such events were key to determining the branching process criticality required for a linearization of the basic reproduction number. Moreover, prior studies on similar spatial models have established conditions for the asymptotic normality of extinction times within infinite populations and identified phase transitions in the lattice dimension related to the "cluster of infection" size under the conditional extinction event. However, those earlier works did not characterize the asymptotic spatial distribution of populations after extinction, a gap this paper addresses directly. While the assumption of a primitive infection probability matrix represents a strong condition, it facilitates the application of a reflection principle, which is essential for proving the main results. These findings are relevant to various fields, including the management of infectious diseases, the analysis of contact processes, and percolation theory.

While prior research has established the existence of this issue, our work conducts novel investigations to quantify the bias, identify its root causes, and propose mitigation strategies. First, we establish quantitative metrics to measure $B_{\perp}$ bias across both local physical components and native image-plane components. Second, we systematically evaluate various inversion methods and data sources, explicitly incorporating the magnetic fill fraction ($ff$), to characterize the impact of these choices. Third, we utilize a simple model to examine how noise and different bias models manifest. Our findings indicate that although the bias predominantly affects under-resolved structures, it also occurs in strong-field pixels that are fully filled. While magnetogram noise can worsen the problem, it is not the primary driver. We demonstrate that explicitly fitting $ff$ offers significant mitigation, though other factors, such as $\chi^2$ weighting and optimization algorithms, also influence results. Furthermore, we present a simple "quick fix" applicable post-facto before resolving the 180° ambiguity in $B_{\perp}$, which is particularly useful when global structures serve as model boundary inputs. These conclusions support the adoption of inversion codes that explicitly fit $ff$ or, as seen with the new SyntHIA neural network, are trained on data derived using this approach. Additionally, we emphasize the need for future studies examining other influencing factors, such as the quality of intensity data and the accuracy of other physical components. Overall, our results underscore that while $B_{\perp}$ remains inherently more uncertain than line-of-sight magnetic field ($B_{\rm los}$), adopting appropriate inversion methods can reduce the bias to levels comparable to the noise in the input magnetogram.

Consequently, there is a critical requirement for algorithms capable of efficiently identifying near-optimal hyperparameters that maximize privacy-utility tradeoffs within a defined search space. This study formulates the issue as a general optimization framework to achieve desirable privacy-utility balances and systematically evaluates three cost-effective algorithms within this context: evolutionary, Bayesian, and reinforcement learning. Extending prior research, we fit median [X/Mg] versus [Mg/H] trends using a two-process model that separates abundance patterns into a "prompt" component linked to core-collapse supernovae and a "delayed" component associated with Type Ia supernovae. For individual stars, we determine the amplitudes of these two components and calculate residuals, denoted as \Delta[X/H], from the resulting two-parameter fit. The root-mean-square residuals span approximately 0.01–0.03 dex for the most precise APOGEE measurements, rising to about 0.1 dex for Na, V, and Ce. Correlation analyses of these residuals expose a complex underlying structure, featuring a correlated group of Ca, Na, Al, K, Cr, and Ce, alongside a distinct group comprising Ni, V, Mn, and Co. Identifying stars that the two-process model fits poorly uncovers a diverse array of physical outliers and occasionally subtle measurement errors. While the majority of these outliers are extremely metal-poor or enhanced in specific elements—typically [X/Mg] > 0.5—some subpopulations with intermediate abundances also emerge. These findings include main-sequence and giant stars, as well as asymptotic giant branch (AGB) and white dwarf progenitors. When analyzed, the residuals from the two-process fit for AGB stars reveal a clear anti-correlation in C and s-process elements (the Mg-Ag anti-correlation), along with a secondary correlation among C, Ni, and V. We conclude by suggesting applications for these two-process fits in future APOGEE analyses, such as identifying variable stars, assessing the binary fraction, and probing the initial conditions of Type Ia supernovae. This analysis demonstrates that a model utilizing two elements (Mg and Fe) to represent a third (Na), as commonly practiced in population studies, can encode intricate abundance patterns arising from multiple physical processes. Consequently, high-resolution, precise abundances for key elements like Na, Cr, and Ce can now be derived for large populations of AGB stars and white dwarf progenitors. -19 pandemic rapidly spread globally, causing severe repercussions in China. During this period, online rumors heightened public anxiety regarding health and social stability, making the detection and containment of such misinformation an urgent priority. To address this, we investigated rumor propagation mechanisms and developed a method to quantify a rumor's influence based on the velocity of new adopters, utilizing search frequency as the primary metric. By analyzing this search frequency, which follows an exponential distribution, we calculated both peak and attenuation coefficients. These coefficients were then treated as target labels for several engineered rumor features. In a 5-fold cross-validation experiment employing mean square error (MSE) as the loss function, decision trees proved optimal for predicting the peak coefficient, while linear regression was ideal for the attenuation coefficient. Feature analysis revealed that precursor attributes were most critical for predicting the outbreak coefficient, whereas location and entity information were paramount for the attenuation coefficient. Furthermore, features that accelerate the initial outbreak often hinder sustained spread, and anxiety was identified as a key driver of rumor generation. Finally, we explored how deep learning techniques, specifically the Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) model, can be leveraged to minimize forecast errors. This study offers practical, evidence-based insights and suggestions for government agencies to effectively manage rumor control. The dataset and code utilized in this study are publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5334/ijnl.13. We hope these findings and resources are beneficial to the broader community. Leveraging these catalogued PNe, we derived independent distance estimates for each galaxy by fitting the observed PNLF while rigorously accounting for detection incompleteness. These individual measurements yield an average distance to the Fornax cluster of 19.86 $\pm$ 0.32 Mpc ($\mu_{PNLF}$ = 31.49 $\pm$ 0.04 mag). To address incompleteness, we developed a novel approach that models the relation between the number of source detections and the magnitude limit as a function of I-band signal-to-noise ratios within each MUSE aperture, based on the distribution of stellar magnitudes in those apertures. the loss function plays a pivotal role, yet selecting the appropriate one remains challenging due to the vast array of available options. Despite this, related studies often fail to provide rigorous justifications for their specific choices, suggesting a dogmatic approach within the deep learning community that lacks empirical grounding. This work investigates supervised classification tasks to evaluate how loss function selection influences training outcomes. Although some functions yield suboptimal results, our empirical analysis demonstrates that underutilized losses, such as KL Divergence, can significantly surpass state-of-the-art alternatives. These findings underscore the necessity of treating the loss function as a tunable hyperparameter rather than adopting it as a fixed default. By systematically evaluating all possible functions, researchers can bypass lucky accidents and make fully informed decisions. We document our empirical results in a public dataset, enabling future studies to leverage these insights. Furthermore, our analysis offers theoretical explanations for these observations and clarifies the conditions under which specific losses are most effective. To utilize this dataset, one may employ the accompanying Python package or explore it directly on Google Colab.

Since this phenomenon markedly affects both the thermal and mechanical characteristics of these materials, it must be accounted for in manufacturing planning and product applications. To simultaneously represent both effects, the proposed model employs a triple decomposition of the deformation gradient. Furthermore, it utilizes a thermodynamic framework grounded in the Coleman–Noll procedure and the principle of minimum dissipation potential, which necessitates specific assumptions regarding the Helmholtz free energy and the dissipation potential. Using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism, we compute the Zeeman contribution to magnetic susceptibility for both chiral and nematic superconducting states close to the critical temperature ($T_c$). The superconducting order parameter, belonging to the $E_u$ representation, couples non-trivially with the transverse Zeeman field, generating a paramagnetic response to magnetization. Furthermore, the Fermi surface topology significantly impacts magnetic susceptibility; a Lifshitz transition shifting the Fermi surface from closed to open drives a phase transition from the nematic to the chiral state, causing the magnetic susceptibility to diverge at this critical point. Additionally, we analyze how electron-electron interactions influence the competition between these phases, finding that in real systems, such interactions can only induce a transition from nematic to chiral states near the phase boundary. Finally, our findings are compared against available experimental data. This work employs a specific model for magnetism within the $E_u$ symmetry sector, based on a previously proposed mechanism for the origin of topological surface states in bi-sesquioxide doped TIs. The proposed mechanism offers a distinct scenario for the origin of topological surface states, potentially elucidating the origin of chiral symmetry breaking and possibly, within the $E_u$ order parameter regime, the anomalous Hall effect observed in these systems.

This was originally established by computing noise kernels, which represent the correlators of the stress-energy tensor for quantum fields. This paper revisits the topic using a quantum thermodynamic framework, specifically calculating two key quantities: heat capacity and quantum compressibility for model geometries containing quantum fields at both high and low temperatures. Heat capacity at constant volume serves as a measure of energy density fluctuations relative to the mean; when this ratio reaches or exceeds one, the applicability of the canonical distribution becomes doubtful. Similarly, compressibility at constant pressure acts as a test for the validity of the grand canonical ensemble. We derive the free energy density to obtain expressions for these thermodynamic quantities for thermal and quantum fields across various spacetimes, including 2D Casimir space, the 2D Einstein cylinder, and the 4D ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe. To explore dimensional dependence, we also derived these quantities for Einstein universes with even spatial dimensions ($S^1 \times S^2$ and $S^1 \times S^4$). This collection of spacetimes allows us to assess the thermodynamic stability of quantum matter fields and draw qualitative conclusions regarding the compatibility conditions necessary for the coexistence of quantum fields and spacetimes, a central challenge in constructing a theory of quantum gravity. This endeavor requires a reformulation of the first and zeroth laws of thermodynamics to account for energy density fluctuations. We observe that for a generic 2D quantum thermal field, the ratio of heat capacity fluctuations to the mean at constant volume exceeds one. Furthermore, we establish that the ratio of compressibility fluctuations to the mean at constant pressure for a generic 4D (S$^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe at high temperatures exceeds one. These results indicate that determining the precise conditions under which quantum fields and spacetimes can coexist within a quantum thermodynamic setting remains an open problem. The outcomes presented here could prove useful in investigating the fundamental principles governing the emergence of spacetime from quantum matter fields to develop a theory of quantum gravity. Unlike existing resources that primarily focus on logical inference rules (if X, then Y), ATOMIC emphasizes diverse inferential knowledge types, including causation, temporal succession, entailed modifications, explanatory relations, complementarity, generalizations, and various other forms of "because" reasoning. This richness enables robust evaluation of AI systems' capacity to infer and explain across multiple knowledge domains. To systematically categorize inferential knowledge, we developed a framework covering seven categories and 27 subcategories of "because" relations. The resource includes structured data in both text and knowledge graph formats, with numerous examples illustrated by pairs of sentence completions (because A, B). ATOMIC was constructed by analyzing over 170,000 dialogue transcripts from the DailyDialog dataset; we detail this creation process, which involves multi-turn conversations where one participant prompts the other to generate inferential knowledge. We ensure high-quality annotations through rigorous validation, including back-translation checks and assessments of annotation agreement. ### 1. Introduction

Understanding pronoun coreference is fundamental to parsing multi-sentence texts. While numerous studies have examined the factors influencing coreference (Riedel et al., 2010; Yang and Snover, 2019) and developed neural models to address it (Tuggener and Riedel, 2015; Yang and Snover, 2Centering; Riedel et al., 2010; Tuggener and Riedel, 2015; Yang and Snover, 2019). Despite this, there remains a lack of consensus on whether coreference and centering are truly distinct phenomena or if they overlap significantly enough to suggest a unified theoretical framework. This uncertainty hinders the selection of optimized contexts for coreference tasks and obscures whether utterance-level context offers valuable information. This paper addresses these questions by explicitly defining centering instances and assessing their impact across various discourse measures.

We also address truthfulness concerns, demonstrating how certain algorithms can be made truthful via VCG-like payments. Furthermore, we define and analyze the "price of serial dictatorship," a metric offering an optimistic assessment of the solution quality produced by action sequences in combinatorial optimization. Finally, we present experimental results comparing our approaches to various algorithms, including those yielding a square-root approximation of social welfare. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/BaruchElian/Serial_Dictatorship.

To facilitate this study, we utilize Dungeons and Dragons (D&D) as our experimental platform; this role-playing game involves multiple player characters and a Dungeon Master (DM) who work together to reach shared objectives beneficial to the players. In this context, each player character represents a student with unique personas and capabilities, while the DM acts as the teacher, serving as the barrier and gateway to the "world." This setup offers a controlled environment to examine grounded communication strategies essential for achieving collective goals. We develop a system model to articulate the constraints and capabilities of all participants and the world entities within a D&D session, thereby defining the semantic space of the game. This model enables the training of a large language model (LLM) to function as a non-player character (NPC) within the D&D universe. The NPC is designed to be goal-oriented, adaptive, and capable of expressing its underlying world model through language. By pairing this NPC with a human DM, we establish a simplified "1v1" scenario to analyze how a student's (the DM's) communication is influenced by the LLM's (the NPC's) world model within a grounded setting. This "1v1" scenario is established to systematically evaluate the factors determining a player character's (the DM's) guided communication. Furthermore, to broadly and deeply understand the grounding of a player character's (the DM's) communication, we propose an "n1v1" scenario where a player character (the DM) interacts with multiple LLM-based (NPC) characters to accomplish a shared objective. Leveraging the log data from these 1v1 and n1v1 scenarios, we demonstrate that a DM's communication can be modeled as a combination of (i) the player character's goals, (ii) the distinctions among player characters, and (iii) the relevant world elements required to reach those goals. Ultimately, our objective is to utilize these experimental findings to ultimately train a more capable and grounded player character model. The code associated with this project can be found at https://github.com/yh0815/CVPR2021-Game2Study.

Assuming the transmitted sequence lies at a distance $d$ from a code and that each channel introduces no more than $r$ errors, the goal is to determine the minimum number of channels necessary to uniquely recover the original sequence. This number must exceed $k_r$, the smallest integer $k$ for which the sum of binomial coefficients $\sum_{i=0}^{r} \binom{k-i}{r}$ exceeds $d$. This article investigates the average case scenario where errors follow independent uniform distributions over an alphabet of size $q$. We begin by outlining the fundamental characteristics of the classic Kermack-McKendrick models before exploring their generalizations and applications to contact networks, viral co-circulation, epidemic curve trajectories, probability distributions, and passage times required to define compartments in these models. Collectively, these examples underscore that a system of differential equations designed for a specific epidemiological challenge relies fundamentally on the epidemiological, medical, and biological context driving its formulation and analysis. Merely fitting differential models to data without considering biological feasibility may yield statistically significant results but will ultimately fail to offer actionable insights for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. We also discuss the limitations of using differential models to predict individual cases, trajectories, or precise peaks, particularly when statistical metrics like R0, Rmax, or the final percentage of the population becoming infected are used to compare regional responses. These findings are especially pertinent as pandemic passage times shift priorities for managing, mitigating, or controlling the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Finally, we argue that employing probabilistic, statistical, or data-driven models, rather than sole reliance on differential models, may better address the inherent complexity, uncertainty, and challenges of the evolving SARS-CoV-2 epidemic. Ultimately, we conclude that mathematicians and statisticians collaborating closely with epidemiologists, engineers, and scientists will most effectively develop novel methodologies and models to address the inherent complexities of the SARS-CoV-2 epidemic and its impact on society. This paper is intended to educate readers on the appropriate context for utilizing different mathematical approaches to study epidemic dynamics. Various abbreviations are defined throughout the text as needed.

Specifically, we analyze how, under appropriate dark-state conditions, the interaction between spin-exchange collisions and photoassociation facilitates the stable formation of atom-molecule pairs from three initial spin-zero atoms. This mechanism, involving two distinct two-body interactions, can be conceptually understood as an effective three-body recombination. We explore the respective influences of photoassociation and initial magnetization in the "resonant" scenario where the dark-state condition is perfectly met. Additionally, we investigate the "non-resonant" regime, where this condition is either approximately fulfilled (the adiabatic case) or not met at all. In the adiabatic scenario, we develop an effective non-rigid pendulum model that enables a clear discussion of the emergence of antiferromagnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum," alongside phenomena such as large-amplitude pair oscillations and atom-molecule entanglement. We also address the Scrooge effect within this context. Furthermore, we utilize a mean-field theory based on the Ginzburg-Landau approximation to investigate these effects in the quasi-condensate regime. This approach reveals the emergence of unstable "atom-molecule polymers" and explores the scaling behaviors of relevant characteristics. Our findings suggest that the laboratory-scale realization of the Scrooge effect, as well as the generation of complex entangled states like the atom-molecule pendulum and its subsequent manipulation, is feasible for bosonic isotopes of Rubase ($^{87}$Rb) and magnetized spin-1 Bose-Einstein condensates of Fermium ($^{140}$Ce). These results may inspire future experiments on similar atom-molecule systems composed of different isotopes or species of spin-1 bosons. Additionally, we propose that the effective non-rigid pendulum model presented here could be implemented using purely atomic systems.

While the Shallow Water Equations (SWEs) are standard for this task, conventional numerical solvers are computationally intensive and depend on high-resolution bathymetry data. This study introduces a two-stage framework: first, we employ the Principal Component Geostatistical Approach (PCGA) to derive the probability density function of bathymetry from flow velocity data, followed by the application of machine learning (ML) algorithms to create a rapid SWE solver. This fast solver utilizes realizations from the posterior bathymetry distribution and prescribed boundary conditions (BCs). The initial stage enables velocity prediction without direct bathymetry measurements. Moreover, we expand the posterior bathymetry distribution into a broader class of distributions before feeding them into the ML model in the second stage. This enhancement allows the solver to integrate future direct bathymetry measurements, improving prediction accuracy even when the riverbed changes over time compared to the initial indirect assessment. We develop and benchmark three distinct solvers—PCA-DNN (Principal Component Analysis-Deep Neural Network), SE (Supervised Encoder), and SVE (Supervised Variational Encoder)—validating them using data from the Savannah River in Augusta, GA. Our findings demonstrate that these fast solvers can predict flow velocities across varying bathymetries and boundary conditions with high accuracy, at a computational cost significantly lower than that of solving the full boundary value problem using FEM (Finite Element Method) solvers. Furthermore, incorporating direct bathymetry measurements in a sequential updating framework further reduces prediction errors, even when the riverbed evolves over time. Consequently, these fast solvers are especially valuable for applications requiring high-frequency flow velocity nowcasting, including flood event monitoring and drone navigation. However, it is crucial to recognize the solver's limitations, specifically the assumption of largely stationary bathymetries over short intervals, which may not hold in highly turbulent events like floods. To address this, we propose a workaround involving a updated (posterior) bathymetry distribution derived from recent velocity measurements (e.g., from sonar or drone sensors). We outline the necessary adjustments to the solver for this scenario and assess its feasibility using synthetic data. Overall, this research offers a significant advancement over previous velocity prediction methods by integrating both indirect and direct bathymetry measurements. Additionally, the generalizable ML solvers developed here can be adapted to predict flows in new river segments with minimal recalibration data.

significant and emerging subfield within machine learning, focused on embedding causal knowledge into the highly adaptable spaces of deep learning architectures. Successfully integrating these causal structures promises more robust, generalizable, and informed predictions and inference. However, the field remains nascent, particularly regarding how to evaluate disparate methods that differ vastly in their output formats, encoding mechanisms, and representation strategies. This living paper extends Pearl's ladder of causation by refining its levels and introducing a new dimension to categorize parametric assumptions for both inputs and representations, thereby creating a comprehensive map of causal deep learning. This framework encompasses various machine learning domains, including supervised learning, reinforcement learning, and generative modeling. Designed as a research tool, the map assists scholars in locating benchmarks, comparing methodologies, and, crucially, identifying gaps in current research. While the volume of published work on CDL grows daily, this map remains static. We have open-sourced the map to facilitate its use by the community, whether for structuring related work sections or more effectively highlighting specific contributions.

This category represents the most fundamental class of maps adhering to a version of the $h$-principle; in two dimensions, it closely approximates oriented submersions, as every such map of dimension 2 targeting a closed, simply connected manifold is bordant to a submersion. We demonstrate that the Madsen-Weiss theorem (the standard Mumford Conjecture) operates within a broader framework of the $h$-principle. Specifically, a version of the $h$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions, when combined with the Harer stability theorem and the Miller-Morita theorem, yields the Madsen-Weiss theorem. The latter can be viewed as the statement that the composition of the stable mapping class group of a surface with one boundary component, denoted $\mathcal{E}_g$, and the Givental symplectic form is bordant to a zero section. This result extends to a generalized Mumford conjecture concerning the $h$-principle for closed symplectic mappings. Furthermore, an version of the $h$-principle for oriented colored broken submersions targeting a symplectic manifold generalizes the long-standing result by Penner and Stashke (1987), which asserts that the composition of the natural map from $\mathcal{E}_g$ to the mapping class group of a closed surface and the symplectic form associated with a surface of minimal genus embedded in a given manifold is zero. This provides a novel and, we believe, more straightforward proof of the Penner-Stashke result. Additionally, an analogous conclusion holds for the Givental symplectic form. The paper also includes a version of the $h$principle for Morse functions targeting a closed contact manifold, which generalizes a theorem by Penner. The work was developed while visiting the Institut de Math\'ematiques de Jussieu in Paris. This visit was made possible through the generous hospitality of the IH\'ES and the IH^M. I am grateful to the IH^M for their kind invitation and warm hospitality.

Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) preconditioners applied to cardiac mechanics on both structured and unstructured finite element meshes. Myocardial mechanical behavior is modeled using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, which are discretized via finite elements to generate large-scale nonlinear algebraic systems. These systems are solved using a Newton-Krylov method, with BDDC/AMG preconditioners accelerating the resolution of the Jacobian linear systems. To ensure a fair comparison, we comprehensively investigate key BDDC parameters, specifically examining the performance of various direct solvers for local and coarse problems, the effects of different choices for BDDC primal degrees of freedom, and the impact of finite element order. Scalability assessments were conducted on Linux clusters utilizing up to 1024 processors, culminating in a performance analysis of a realistic electromechanical simulation. The findings reveal that, unlike computational fluid dynamics, cardiac mechanics do not significantly benefit from replacing the direct solvers used in BDDC with AMG techniques. Furthermore, an aggressive mesh refinement analysis demonstrates that an appropriately configured BDDC preconditioner outperforms AMG in terms of both solution time and scalability. Overall, Jacobian systems are solved in approximately 2 seconds per step, and the simulation of a Q1 mesh takes 19 hours using 96 processors. These results indicate that BDDC maintains constant performance per finite element for the examined problem, making it highly effective for cardiac mechanics simulations.

Because this approach is independent of specific geometries or mode bases, it serves as a versatile foundation for analyzing phenomena arising from any mix of linear coupling, scattering, and Kerr nonlinearity. These include losses due to bending and surface roughness, geometric backscattering, self- and cross-phase modulation, four-wave mixing, third-harmonic generation, and Kerr frequency comb generation. The framework is subsequently applied to a translationally symmetric waveguide to compute the evanescent coupling strength between the waveguide and a nearby microresonator, as well as the Kerr self- and cross-phase modulation terms within the resonator. Finally, this enables the derivation of a dimensionless equation governing the symmetry-breaking dynamics of two counterpropagating modes in a loop resonator, demonstrating that cross-phase modulation is precisely twice as strong as self-phase modulation only when the two counterpropagating modes are otherwise identical. Finally, we propose potential updates to the formulation necessary to incorporate directional couplers and asymmetric joints. This explicit, geometry-independent description of all order-$O(\beta)$ and $O(\beta^2)$ effects provides a significant improvement over standard coupled-mode theory, which typically relies on approximate mode bases that often fail to capture nonreciprocal scattering losses and cross-Kerr effects between modes. Our results can be easily extended to more complex structures, such as ring resonators with elliptical or arbitrary asymmetries, to yield an explicit description of all relevant linear and Kerr nonlinear coupling terms, including cross-phase modulation between the clockwise and counterclockwise propagating modes. These outcomes are directly applicable to the analysis of the stability and pattern formation of counterpropagating beams in the near-field of optical loop resonators and to the understanding of cross-pump Kerr comb generation in microresonators. The presented formalism also facilitates the efficient and accurate computation of the parameters required in a truncated counterpropagating coupled-mode equation (CME) model for simulating near-field dynamics in optical loop resonators and the associated experimental setups. This is achieved with considerably lower computational cost, numerical noise, and geometric symmetry breaking concerns compared to standard methods based on Finite Difference Time Domain (FDTD) or Finite Element Method (FEM) simulations. Consequently, the reported findings enable the rapid and reliable calculation of the parameters needed in a symmetric CME model for the near-field dynamics of co-propagating fields in optical loop resonators, overcoming the limitations of current approximate models

To examine how bulges influence the MS, we analyzed the NUV$-r$ color—a reliable tracer of specific star formation rate—in the central ($r<R_{50}$) versus outer regions of 6,401 local star-forming galaxies. Our results show that for galaxies with $M_{\ast}<10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ is only about 0.25 magnitudes redder than the outer regions. However, above $M_{\ast}=10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, the central NUV$-r$ becomes significantly redder than the outer regions, indicating that bulges in massive galaxies are more evolved. When sorting galaxies by S\'ersic index $n$, those with $n>2.5$ exhibit redder central NUV$-r$ colors than those with $n<2.5$, even when controlling for B/T ratio and $M_{\ast}$. Furthermore, the fraction of galaxies with $n>2.5$ and a given B/T ratio is more substantial at higher masses. These findings regarding the NUV$-r$ color are consistent with previous observations using the $g-r$ color. Consequently, the majority of bulges in low-mass galaxies are compact and actively forming stars, whereas bulges in massive galaxies are more quiescent. We conclude that the buildup of bulges in massive galaxies occurs through the inside-out growth of the disc, rather than the outside-in accretion of clumpy satellites. This is because an accretion mechanism would imply that bulges with specific histories should be uniformly active across all galaxies, which contradicts our data. We confirm that the positive slope of the MS is not caused by bulge expansion. The shift from inside-out to outside-in growth modes at $M_{\ast}\sim 10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$ marks a transition in star formation efficiency, where radiative cooling in the gas compared to radiative thermal conduction plays a critical role. This constitutes a previously unreported mechanism for the "knee" in the MS.

We note that training is hindered by a skewed relationship proposal distribution, where most negative proposals are easily detected due to inaccurate object detection, causing the model to underfit rare, difficult cases. To address this, we introduce Spatially-Aware Balanced negative pRoposal sAmpling (SABRA), a robust VRD framework designed to mitigate false positive impacts. Visual relationship detection (VRD) is a critical yet underexplored task in computational photography, computing a list of plausible (object$_i$, preposition, object$_j$) triplets within an image. Despite its apparent simplicity, SABRA identifies and mitigates a primary source of errors in existing VRD systems: the high volume of false positives. In this study, we analyze the root causes of these false positives and propose a SABRA framework to resolve the issue. Firstly, we address the imbalanced training distribution problem by introducing a Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling mechanism. This approach balances the training distribution by sampling negative proposals from their original distributions, creating a smoother landscape for optimization and significantly reducing false positive counts. Secondly, we enhance the model's spatial reasoning by integrating a graph-based object interaction modeling module (MH-GAT) and a light-weight spatial mask decoder. These components respectively capture global and local spatial object configurations, specifically targeting low-frequency, challenging false positives. Experimental results across two HOI and one general VRD datasets confirm that our method significantly reduces false positives compared to state-of-the-art approaches. The SABRA

imeter observations of three massive ($>10^{11}\,\rm M_{\odot}$), highly star-forming galaxies located in the core of the RO-1001 group at redshift $z=2.91$. Each galaxy features compact, kiloparsec-scale starburst cores with characteristics indicative of forming bulges, situated within extended, massive stellar disks. Notably, these disks are both distinctly quiescent and severely asymmetric. This configuration suggests that "outside-in" quenching is actively occurring in these group members. We propose a scenario where the significant mass asymmetry in the disks (varying by factors of 1.6 to over 3), likely induced by accreted gas and clumps, suppresses star formation in the outer regions while channeling gas toward the nuclei to fuel central starbursts. The asymmetric side of the disks indicates the impact site of accretion streams, with nearby dust and stellar components directly tracing the inflow direction. Interactions with these accreted clumps, viewed as minor mergers, align the major axes of the three galaxies with external Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting feeding filaments. These findings offer the first observational proof of how cold accretion streams influence galaxy formation and evolution. Currently, this process manifests as the rapid assembly of bulges driven by accretion, while maintaining massive, quiescent, and highly asymmetric disks. Direct detections of associated gas and dust components demonstrate that the incoming cold accretion streams branch off from larger Lyman-$\alpha$-emitting structures. While the full development of this "merger-driven asymmetric monolithic collapse" scenario is still underway, producing galaxies with "seedy" bulges and massive disks, its completion will result in massive, classical bulge-plus-disk galaxies. Such formations are essential for explaining the abundance of red, massive galaxies observed at $z>2$. The general applicability of this "differential star formation" process in shaping the populations of massive galaxies is strongly supported by the similar mass asymmetries seen in the disks of these $z=2-3$ galaxies. This mechanism, termed "merger-driven asymmetric monolithic collapse," can rapidly build up bulges while regulating outer star formation during the assembly of massive galaxies, thereby accounting for the presence of red, massive galaxies with established bulges at high redshifts.

Bolivia (5250 m a.s.l.) and Mexico (4600 m a.s.l.) detected a notable event on November 7, 2004, linked to an X2.0-class solar flare. Data from our records, alongside observations from GOES 11 and SOHO satellites, indicate that electrons and protons—potential byproducts of neutron decay—were present. While solar neutron decay protons (sndp) were previously detected aboard the ISEE3 satellite on June 3, 1982, and by ground-level instruments in Goose Bay and Deep River on October 19, 1989, this marks the second instance of such evidence being recorded directly on Earth's surface. Our measurements yield a decay angle of 73 ± 2 degrees and a decay height of 23 ± 2 degrees, which align well with expectations derived from the detection location's latitude and the event's maximum elevation angle. Furthermore, the sndp count observed in our instruments is consistent with a production rate of approximately 10 per second at an angle of 90 degrees. We also observed a ground-level neutron count excursion, which, unlike the effects of a Ground Level Enhancement (GLE), exhibited a gradual buildup rather than a sudden onset. This gradual progression suggests a different physical origin, possibly related to p-p or n-n interactions. These findings collectively demonstrate that high-altitude neutron telescopes are capable of detecting solar neutron decay protons, an event that typically manifests only transiently and intensifies as the source approaches its nadir position. While low- and intermediate-mass stars typically exhibit rigid rotation on the main sequence, stellar evolution into the giant phase—characterized by core contraction and envelope expansion—generally predicts a profile with a rapidly rotating core and slowly rotating envelope, assuming initial rigid rotation. However, observations of the larger giants often contradict this, showing a profile closer to rigid rotation. We analyze high-resolution spectroscopic data for the giant $\chi^1$ Cet and estimate its surface rotation rate, core rotation velocity (assuming rigid-like behavior up to the photosphere), and the base of the convective zone. The data suggest that $\chi^1$ Cet possesses a counter-intuitive profile, rotating faster at the surface than in the sub-photospheric layers. While this suggests an instability during the main-sequence stage of $\chi^1$ Cet that could explain this anomaly, the observed effect is modest, making it difficult to account for with a simple model of stellar evolution from initial rigid rotation. Furthermore, while magnetic activity is known to induce differential rotation in rapid rotors like the Twarriga stars, $\chi^1$ Cet's relatively low activity levels, the lack of constraints on the activity-induced differential rotation magnitude, and the stellar envelope's high opacity make this mechanism unlikely to explain the result. Consequently, we suggest that the rotation profile of $\chi^1$ Cet may indeed be nonmonotonic, representing a rare instance where main-sequence evolutionary timescales failed to establish a expected differentially rotating state. This star serves as an ideal candidate for detailed modeling of differential rotation and the influence of magnetic activity, potentially allowing for the investigation of the main-sequence timescale required to generate a prominent differential rotation signal as the envelope expands. $\chi^1$ Cet could aid in calibrating surface rotation measurement techniques reliant on spectral line broadening, thereby enabling the detection of differential rotation in greater number of main-sequence stars. Additionally, if the enhanced surface rotation is attributed to core contraction, the inferred core rotation rate is notably lower than the expected value from simple contraction timescales, implying the presence of an inertial timescale within the star comparable to the contraction timescale.

Although graph neural networks (GNNs) offer a valuable relational inductive bias for modeling these systems, research into their ability to generalize to new instances within the same system type remains limited. In this study, we trained GNNs to learn time series data from a specific nonlinear dynamical system known as the belief propagation algorithm. Our analysis revealed that the learned representations and model components have straightforward interpretations that align with the fundamental properties of probabilistic inference. We successfully developed a "graph translator" that maps statistical interactions in belief propagation to the parameters of the trained network. This translator facilitates two forms of novel generalization: reconstructing the underlying structure of a new system instance using only time series observations, or directly building a new network from that structure. These findings illustrate a pathway to comprehending both the dynamics and structure of complex systems and demonstrate how such insights can drive generalization. The methods described here are applicable to any system whose state can be represented graphically. Prior to our work, the feasibility of generalizing GNNs to new system instances beyond their training distribution was unproven, and the learning of data structures like those in belief propagation remained an open challenge. Building on this research, we introduce a methodology to teach GNNs the dynamics of Ising models, thereby achieving generalization to new Ising model instances.

Complex systems are defined by the numerous ways their components can interact. Neural networks, including brain regions, serve as a primary example. While GNNs provide a necessary inductive bias for learning from time series data in such systems, it remains unclear whether a GNN trained on one system can generalize to a new instance of the same system type. Traditional generalization only applies when some input (like an image) comes from the same distribution, which is not the case here. Addressing this, we show that a GNN can learn the structure of a new system instance given its time series, utilizing the "soft constraints" inherent in the network's architecture. This allows the model to generate data consistent with observed time series, effectively treating structure learning as a constraint satisfaction problem guided by the learned representations. To validate this, we trained a GNN on the belief propagation dynamic—a generic process governing many statistical systems—using a synthetic dataset. The results confirm that the network learns representations and parts consistent with the algorithm's intuitionistic nature. Most significantly, we proved that a network trained on a single graph can accurately reconstruct and learn the structure of a new, unseen graph from that same distribution. Deep learning techniques have gained significant adoption in medical image analysis due to their superior classification and segmentation capabilities. However, training these models often requires vast amounts of data and extensive computational resources, which are frequently unattainable in clinical settings. Transfer learning has been utilized to overcome these hurdles by leveraging pre-trained networks on large-scale datasets; nevertheless, this approach is ineffective when the source and target domains differ significantly. In such scenarios, this paper introduces a new method that adapts a teacher network from few-shot continuous adaptation. This approach enhances the teacher network using patient-specific data without compromising its generalization skills, thereby avoiding the high costs associated with retraining from scratch. To implement this, we employ neuro-symbolic knowledge representation to capture knowledge from both training and test samples, enabling the model to recognize new patients and adapt efficiently with as few as five new images. This method is particularly advantageous for longitudinal analysis of a single patient or for classifying new patients with only a few-shot samples. Experimental results on the ORL face dataset and a real-world ECG dataset (including the PTB-XD dataset and a 78-case patient-specific ECG dataset) demonstrate that the proposed approach surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. The source code for this project is available at https://github.com/HKU-MMKL/DSL.

Anti-aliasing for line joins (intersecting road segments) enhances the visual appeal of vector maps and is critical for real-time map rendering performance. Navigation cues embedded in 360-degree video content can help estimate user viewports. Quantum mechanics fundamentally relies on the linearity of Hilbert spaces, yet its physical states are represented by linear rays—collections of vectors related by complex scaling—within these spaces. While the physical content is invariant under changes of representative vectors, many phenomena, such as quantum phase transitions, are better understood by examining the geometric arrangement of these rays. This approach has been especially valuable in the study of quantum entanglement. In this work, we extend the concept of geometric quantum mechanics to infinite quantum systems, whose states are described not by Hilbert spaces but by type III$_1$ von Neumann algebras, which lack non-trivial superselection sectors. To achieve this, we employ the physically significant KMS ray associated with an interaction, which connects the quantum states of two thermally linked subsystems. Because this ray is defined by the dynamics of the combined system, it encapsulates the entanglement inherent in the subsystems when they are at finite temperature. We establish that two such infinite, interacting systems are thermally equivalent precisely when their associated KMS rays are unitarily equivalent. Additionally, we illustrate how dynamics in quantum many-body systems can also be analyzed through the evolution of these rays. Finally, we show that a general form of Goldstone's theorem applies to excitations arising from symmetry breaking in quantum many-body systems at finite temperatures.
