Transfer learning has been suggested to address these challenges, even when bridging language gaps, such as adapting an English model for German ASR. In this study, we explore transferring an English model to Czech ASR, a task involving languages with lower mutual intelligibility. To streamline this transfer, we introduce the use of an intermediate alphabet—Czech stripped of accents—and demonstrate that this approach is highly effective. This technique also proves beneficial when applied solely to Czech data, resembling a coarse-to-fine training paradigm. Our results show significant reductions in both training time and word error rate (WER). Specifically, the time elapsed from initiation to reaching a certain WER level is approximately halved when using the intermediate alphabet compared to training directly on Czech data. Furthermore, the final WER achieved is lower in the transfer scenario than in the non-transfer case, despite the English corpus being roughly ten times larger than the Czech one. We attribute these gains to the shared structural rules among Slavic languages, which the intermediate alphabet effectively captures. Additionally, the approach requires minimal resources, making it feasible to implement with relatively small English and Czech corpora. Our findings indicate that even languages with low mutual intelligibility can benefit significantly from ASR transfer learning, especially when an intermediate alphabet is employed. The code and models from this project are publicly available at https://github.com/MagdalenaSobolova/ASR_transfer.

Neural machine translation has advanced rapidly, largely due to RNN-based models and the Transformer architecture. Recently, the Transformer's efficacy in end-to-end speech recognition was confirmed, although its massive size hinders deployment on mobile devices or in real-time. This paper proposes a two-stage approach to adapt a pre-trained English machine translation model to Czech speech recognition. The first stage involves translating a English corpus into a intermediate alphabet that represents Czech without diacritics. The second stage adapts this model to Czech data, again utilizing the intermediate alphabet. Experiments using the largest available Czech corpora demonstrate that this method yields a 5 WER percentage point reduction compared to baseline training on Czech alone. By comparing models trained on Croatian, Slovak, and Czech, we analyzed the transfer learning process and found that the intermediate alphabet helps the model focus on the intrinsic structure of Czech. Our results confirm that efficient end-to-end speech recognition is possible by leveraging high-resource foreign languages through intermediate alphabets, and we release both the trained model and code publicly.

In many multi-document coreference resolution (MDCR) tasks, datasets lack sufficient coreferent mentions for every entity, rendering the existing corescriptions inadequate for training models to recognize all potential coreferent expressions. To address this limitation in low-resource MDCR, we propose a data augmentation strategy that leverages sentence-level coreference to expand coreferent mentions. Our evaluation across three distinct low-resource MDCR tasks indicates that this approach consistently enhances model performance. Additionally, we introduce a hierarchical MDCR framework that processes coreferent mentions at both the sentence and paragraph levels, which outperforms current state-of-the-art methods on the full WikiCRF dataset. Our expanded dataset, titled WikiCRF+, is available at https://github.com/zhengry19/WikiCRFplus.

among strategic agents with additive valuations, assuming no monetary transfers. In this context, a mechanism is an algorithm that processes agents' reported valuations rather than their true ones. Our primary objective is to determine if mechanisms exist that guarantee the existence of pure Nash equilibria for every scenario while simultaneously ensuring fairness in the resulting allocations. Specifically, we investigate two relaxations of envy-freeness: envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) and envy-freeness up to any good (EFX), ultimately providing an affirmative answer. We analyze two algorithms recognized for generating such allocations in non-strategic environments: Round-Robin, which yields EF1 allocations for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method by Plaut and Roughgarden [SIAM Journal of Discrete Mathematics, 2020] that produces EFX allocations for two agents. We demonstrate that all pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin result in allocations that are EF1 relative to the agents' true values. Furthermore, we show that the Plaut and Roughgarden algorithm not only achieves EFX but also satisfies maximin share fairness in this strategic setting—a property it does not possess in the non-strategic case. Additionally, we prove that a weaker version of this result applies to any two-agent mechanism that consistently yields pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations. However, we observe that neither algorithm necessarily leads to socially optimal allocations. These findings are significant because they confirm that both algorithms prevent envy up to any item for an arbitrary number of agents when agents act rationally and report truthfully, a property we term weak-EFX. We also define this concept and prove that Round-Robin always yields weak-EFX allocations. Moreover, we present a mechanism for an even number of agents that always results in a strong-EFX allocation. Finally, we discuss implications for the efficiency of allocations generated by these mechanisms. Throughout the paper, we utilize extensive computational simulations to offer further insights, including an observation that Round-Robin often produces allocations that are EFX up to any good for agents with concave valuations. Regarding social welfare, we establish a lower bound showing that equilibrium allocations from any two-agent mechanism achieving weak-EFX are at least 2/3 as efficient as the optimal allocation, improving upon a previous bound of 5/7 for allocations that are EFX up to one good. Additionally, we prove that pure Nash equilibria of Round-Robin always achieve at least 3/4 of the optimal social welfare

analyzing how mass accretion rates correlate with stellar and disk characteristics. While the scatter in these relationships can refine disk evolution models, this is only possible if accretion variability is properly considered. Although variability is significant during the embedded phases of star formation, it is often assumed to be minor in later stages. In this study, we report substantial accretion rate variations observed in the target XX Cha and discuss their implications for population studies of classical T Tauri stars. Comparing mass accretion rates derived from fitting UV-to-near-infrared spectra in recent X-Shooter observations with those measured 11 years prior using the same instrument, we find that XX Cha exhibits nearly 2 dex of accretion variability between 2010 and 2021. While the specific timescales of this variation remain uncertain, XX Cha demonstrates extreme accretion variability for a classical T Tauri star. If such behavior is common among these stars, potentially occurring in up to 10% of the population, it must be incorporated into statistical models when assessing accretion evolution. Furthermore, the significant variability in XX Cha suggests that the measurement uncertainty inherent in deriving accretion rates from spectral data may be larger than previously estimated. These findings underscore the necessity of directly monitoring individual T Tauri stars to unravel the physical processes governing the evolution of their surrounding disks.

However, practical applications often involve behavior policies generating joint trajectories with varying performance levels; for instance, one agent might follow a random policy while others adhere to medium-quality policies. In cooperative games with global rewards, existing offline MARL approaches often allow agents to inherit these suboptimal random policies, thereby compromising the team's overall performance. This paper investigates offline MARL with explicit attention to the diversity of individual agent trajectories and introduces a novel framework termed Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) to mitigate this issue. Specifically, an attention-based reward decomposition network utilizes a differentiable key-value memory mechanism to assign credit to each agent in an offline setting. These decomposed credits facilitate the reconstruction of joint offline datasets into prioritized experience replay based on individual trajectories, enabling agents to share high-quality experiences. Subsequently, agents conservatively train their policies using a graph attention network (GAT)-based critic. Evaluations across discrete control environments (StarCraft II and multi-agent particle environments) and continuous control settings (multi-agent MuJoCo) demonstrate that our method yields significantly superior results on complex, mixed offline multi-agent datasets, particularly when there are substantial disparities in the quality of individual trajectories. This research offers a new perspective on leveraging individual trajectories in offline multi-agent learning and provides a practical solution for real-world multi-agent system deployments. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/yzh1699/SIT-SORI.

Most conventional intensity-based registration techniques rely on optimization algorithms to maximize image similarity; while these often yield satisfactory results for kilovoltage (kV) images, they struggle with MV images due to inferior image quality and typically lack a sufficient capture range. To address these limitations, we propose employing a CNN. Furthermore, the study confirms that MV images are suitable for image registration with CNNs and aids in determining the optimal network architecture. Conventional registration methods are widely available in clinical practice, with Zephir serving as a prominent example. Building upon successful preliminary results achieved with 3D MRI and kV CT images, we now extend this work to MV images. Our dataset comprises 100 scans, each featuring four distinct viewing angles, which is currently being collected and will eventually include approximately 200 scans. We continue to develop a CNN architecture that leverages the view-invariant properties of patients to reduce the model's dimensionality. This approach is also investigated on a smaller dataset to assess its effectiveness. Our findings indicate that using a 2D/3D CNN for MV image registration is feasible, yields satisfactory results, and that incorporating view invariance helps minimize the required network size. Ultimately, this project aims to establish the proof-of-concept and dataset foundation for developing an automated angle finder for radiotherapy patients based on MV images.

advanced information technology systems has delivered substantial benefits to Internet of Vehicles (IoV) ecosystems, it has simultaneously amplified security and privacy risks. Consequently, privacy preservation methods have become a focal point in academic research to safeguard IoV data. However, these existing approaches require specific adaptations to align with evolving IoV architectures. Meanwhile, Federated Learning (FL) has emerged as a promising solution for enhancing data privacy and security within IoVs. Concurrently, Blockchain technology offers significant potential through its secure, decentralized, and auditable mechanisms for data recording and sharing. This paper provides a comprehensive survey on the application and implementation of Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. Additionally, it examines potential challenges, proposed solutions, and future research directions associated with these frameworks. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational resource for developing modern Blockchain-Enabled FL solutions to address various data privacy issues and scenarios in IoVs. To achieve this, the paper begins by introducing the necessary background on IoVs, AI/FL, and Blockchain technologies. Subsequently, it offers a detailed overview of current research on these solutions, followed by a detailed analysis of problem statements and proposed solutions. Finally, the survey concludes with a summary of key findings. Throughout this process, visual aids and quantitative data are extensively utilized to clarify complex issues and convey the authors' perspectives effectively. Additionally, the paper proposes a new classification scheme for organizing recent studies on these frameworks and highlights recent advancements in this field. By systematically reviewing related work, this survey underscores the significance of these solutions and their potential future research trajectories. Throughout the survey, recent developments are highlighted to contextualize the proposed solution within the broader field of Blockchain-Enabled FL for IoVs. In summary, this survey presents the background, problem statement, related work, and proposed solution regarding Blockchain-Enabled Federated Learning frameworks for IoVs. In the future work section, the necessary improvements and updates required for this survey are outlined. During the offline stage, the base station (BS) fits a GMM to uplink (UL) training data and subsequently generates a codebook in an unsupervised fashion by leveraging the model's clustering properties, assigning one codebook entry to each GMM component. In the online phase, the BS offloads the GMM to the mobile terminal (MT) without transferring the codebook; the MT then uses the GMM to identify the most appropriate codebook entry. This process eliminates the need for channel estimation at the MT, as it relies on the observed signal to calculate the responsibility of each GMM component. Furthermore, the methodology is completely online, avoiding complex offline clustering procedures, which facilitates easy integration with existing systems. The core mechanism involves the GMM, which effectively captures the multi-modal nature of the distribution from which channels are drawn. By assigning one codebook entry to each component, the design ensures that the probability of selecting a specific entry aligns with the probability that the corresponding component generated the observed signal. Finally, the feedback index corresponds to the component with the greatest responsibility, reflecting a decision-theoretic rationale.

investigate Population III (Pop III) binary remnant mergers within nuclear star clusters (NSCs) during the early stages of structure formation. We track the dynamical evolution of Pop III compact object binaries as cosmic structures develop, calculating how field stars' dynamical friction drives these remnants into NSCs. Subsequent evolution inside the clusters is modeled through three-body interactions and gravitational-wave (GW) emission. Our results indicate that 7.5% of Pop III binary remnants will migrate to the galactic centers (within 3 pc). Of these, approximately 5–50% will merge at redshifts greater than zero within NSCs, a process that includes systems with initially large separations (up to 1 pc). The merger rate density (MRD) reaches its peak at $z\sim 5-7$, ranging from $\sim 0.4-10\ \rm yr^{-1}\ \rm Gpc^{-3}$, which translates to a potential detection rate of $\sim 170-2700\ \rm yr^{-1}$ for third-generation GW detectors capable of observing up to $z\sim 10$. The majority ($\gtrsim 90\%$) of these mergers occur in low-mass ($\lesssim 10^{6}\ \rm M_{\odot}$) NSCs formed at high redshifts ($z\gtrsim 3$). While most binaries reach the galactic center with final separations around 1 pc, roughly 1 in every 200 merges occurs in the outer regions of the NSCs. We further analyze how uncertainties in Pop III binary formation, dynamical evolution parameters, and the galactic potential influence the MRD. This work establishes the foundational framework necessary for interpreting future observations of Pop III merger events by advanced GW detectors. Additionally, we examine how third-generation detectors can distinguish these events from solar-metallicity (Pop IV) binary mergers, which may also occur in galactic centers. Pop III binaries are predicted to exhibit smaller mass ratios ($q\lesssim 0.15$) and lower spins ($\lesssim 0.05$) compared to Pop IV remnants. Observing a spin-bias or an excess of mass ratios $q\lesssim 0.2$ among low-redshift ($z\lesssim 1$) heavy black hole (BH) binaries would strongly suggest a Pop III origin.

Text-based games are widely recognized as effective platforms for training and evaluating vision-less agents on fundamental AI skills, including natural language understanding, common-sense reasoning, and programmatic thinking. The Python library TextWorld, released last year, remains the sole existing tool for playing and experimenting with these games. However, due to its relatively slow execution speed—approximately 300 steps per second—it is impractical for conducting large-scale experiments involving modern agents. To address this limitation, we introduce TextWorld-HD, a high-performance library that accelerates simulation by a factor of 100x, enabling the execution of 20 million steps within 24 hours. Our implementation leverages action vectorization to bypass text-based communication bottlenecks, directly transmitting action embeddings between the agent and the environment. Despite this shift to vector-based actions, TextWorld-HD remains fully compatible with TextWorld; thus, any algorithm feasible in TextWorld can likewise be executed in TextWorld-HD. a potent class of deep neural networks extensively applied to sequence analysis and modeling. Nevertheless, their substantial model size hinders practical deployment, particularly in video recognition tasks involving high-dimensional data. To address this constraint and maximize the potential of LSTMs, this paper introduces an algorithm and hardware co-design strategy for high-performance, energy-efficient LSTM networks. At the algorithmic level, we introduce the FDHT-LSTM, a model based on a fully decomposed hierarchical Tucker (FDHT) structure that maintains high accuracy with ultra-low complexity. To leverage these algorithmic advantages, we designed a specialized hardware architecture capable of executing the FDHT-LSTM efficiently. Through a refined memory access scheme, the hardware supports complex matrix transformations in real-time without access conflicts. Evaluation results demonstrate that both the compact FDHT-LSTM models and the dedicated hardware accelerator deliver superior performance. Compared to state-of-the-art compressed LSTMs, FDHT-LSTM offers order-of-magnitude reductions in model size alongside significant accuracy gains across various video recognition datasets. Furthermore, against the state-of-the-art tensor decomposed hardware accelerator TIE, our FDHT-LSTM architecture achieves higher throughput, better area efficiency, and improved energy efficiency on the LSTM-Youtube workload. Similarly, on the LSTM-UCF workload, our design outperforms TIE in throughput and energy efficiency while maintaining comparable area efficiency. To ensure the feasibility of our approach, we detailed the FDHT matrix decomposition process and access patterns, validated the accelerator's correctness through extensive simulations, and verified performance claims using a 28nm NSDS model in HSPICE. To facilitate future research, we released the accelerator's Verilog code along with accurate memory access and data format libraries.

Yet, current assessments and policy guidance on market design and ancillary services often fail to account for the intricate interactions between markets and services. To address this gap, this paper introduces an open-source agent-based model designed to evaluate design options for electricity markets and ancillary services. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model (ASAM) integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA toolbox for power system analysis. A stylized simulation scenario was used to validate the model and explore a specific redispatch design issue. The findings regarding multi-period all-or-none order types in redispatch markets reveal three key implications: (1) The order design minimizes risk for market participants by ensuring full order clearance. (2) Large orders can create dispatch ramps where smaller orders receive electricity at prices exceeding the forecasted production cost. (3) An agent-based approach like ASAM is essential for investigating such issues, as it enables representing strategic behavior and assessing outcomes across extended timeframes, which is impossible with equilibrium models. Furthermore, the validation scenario and its results are intended to assist researchers in exploring other design problems regarding electricity markets and ancillary services. The study concludes by emphasizing the open-source ASAM model's utility for investigating complex issues within the electricity sector.

Although scattered light inherently contains both the amplitude and phase of the electromagnetic field, phase data is frequently discarded during standard intensity measurements. Nevertheless, phase information is often critical for reconstructing target details, a principle established in coherent x-ray imaging. This work presents a novel phase retrieval algorithm capable of recovering field phase data from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra. We demonstrate this technique using x-ray scattering from Mössbauer nuclei at a synchrotron facility. Access to phase data enables a superior reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental results—a level of precision unattainable through conventional methods. Consequently, our approach offers a powerful new tool for data analysis that will advance both x-ray quantum optics and synchrotron-based Mössbauer spectroscopy. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is broadly applicable to any 2D spectral dataset, making it relevant for various coherent x-ray imaging and spectroscopy experiments.

applied to a new hybrid-dimensional model for single-phase Darcy flow in fractured porous media. The model represents fractures as $(d-1)$-dimensional interfaces within a $d$-dimensional domain, where $d$ equals 2 or 3. Fractures are categorized into two types based on the permeability contrast between the fracture and the surrounding matrix: those with significantly higher permeability are termed {\it conductive}, while those with significantly lower permeability are termed {\it blocking}. Conductive fractures are modeled using a standard hybrid-dimensional interface approach assuming continuous pressure across the interface, whereas blocking fractures utilize a recent Dirac-$\delta$ function approach that enforces continuity of the normal Darcy velocity component. A key innovation of this scheme is its ability to handle nonconforming meshes regarding blocking fractures, a capability enabled by the Dirac-$\delta$ formulation. Additionally, the numerical method yields locally conservative velocity approximations and generates a symmetric positive definite linear system defined solely on pressure degrees of freedom located at the mesh skeleton. Benchmark tests in both two and three dimensions demonstrate the method's performance, with results showing it to be highly competitive against existing literature approaches.

Although Bayes factors provide a direct approach to hypothesis evaluation, they are notably sensitive to specific data characteristics and model assumptions. Furthermore, their practical implementation remains uncertain regarding its robustness to computational details. This study examines these issues within the context of cognitive science applications. We clarify the statistical foundations of Bayes factors for Bayesian inference and emphasize the necessity of utility functions for making principled decisions. Additionally, we investigate the behavior of Bayes factors under various conditions, including errors in estimation. Notably, it remains unclear whether bridge sampling yields unbiased estimates for complex analyses; we address this by employing simulation-based calibration for the first time to assess the accuracy of such estimates. Our analysis also covers the stability of Bayes factors across different MCMC samples, their dependence on data variations, and the variability of resulting decisions, proposing methods to optimize these decisions via utility functions. We outline a reproducible workflow for researchers to test the robustness of Bayes factors in their specific analyses, illustrated with a case study from cognitive science. Ultimately, this work aims to provide a framework for evaluating the strengths and limitations of Bayes factors as a metric for scientific evidence. Reproducible code is accessible at https://osf.io/y354c/.

Recent studies have productively investigated predicting discourse markers between sentence pairs to derive accurate sentence representations beneficial for various classification tasks. This paper adopts a different approach: we utilize a model trained to predict discourse markers between sentence pairs to infer plausible markers for pairs with known semantic relations (sourced from existing classification datasets). These inferences enable us to examine the relationship between discourse markers and the semantic relations annotated in these datasets. Although handcrafted mappings have been suggested between markers and discourse relations for limited sets of markers and categories, hundreds of discourse markers express a diverse range of relations, and there is no agreed-upon taxonomy of relations among competing theories (which are predominantly constructed top-down). By employing an automatic prediction method over existing semantically annotated datasets, we offer a bottom-up characterization of discourse markers in English. The resulting dataset, called DiscSense, is publicly accessible. We explore various machine translation models to construct a grammar-based feature set for each marker, which we use to profile the semantic relations expressed by a collection of 1,851 discourse markers across 1,551,851 instances in annotated corpus data. Our analyses reveal that markers are generally polysemous, often expressing multiple related semantic relations, whereas relations are typically monodiscursive, expressed by multiple markers. We also present a coarse-grained clustering of discourse markers based on their expressed relations and provide examples of "by contrast" markers expressing distinct relations, such as concession, antonymy, and a previously undocumented relation, inferiority. Beyond contributing to theoretical discourse analysis, DiscSense serves as a rich resource for researchers interested in the semantics of discourse markers and can be leveraged to enhance NLP tasks, including classification (e.g., sentiment and toxicity) and prediction (e.g., hate speech and profanity). The DiscSense dataset is available at discoursemarkersemantics.com.

By applying the Burer-Monteiro factorization within a specific Riemannian quotient geometry defined on a search space equipped with a Euclidean metric, we analyze the global landscape of the resulting factorized objective. Assuming the original objective function $f$ adheres to standard restricted strong convexity and smoothness conditions, we demonstrate that the entire search space partitions into three distinct regions: (R1) a neighborhood around the target parameter where the objective is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (R2) areas surrounding all strict saddle points; and (R3) remaining regions characterized by large gradients. To our knowledge, this constitutes the first global landscape analysis of the Burer-Monteiro factorized objective under this specific Riemannian quotient geometry. These findings offer a complete geometric rationale for the enhanced performance of vanilla gradient descent in this context. Furthermore, under a weaker restricted strict convexity assumption, we establish that the search space is divided into two regions, with one containing a geodesically restricted convex objective. Numerical experiments align with our theoretical assertions and further reveal that the search space is indeed partitioned by a sphere centered at the optimal parameter. Our assumptions represent the weakest possible conditions required for landscape analysis under the standard definition of restricted strong convexity, as they do not imply strong convexity. Additionally, our results generalize to a broader class of problems involving objectives with a restricted restricted convex-like landscape. This generalization encompasses existing results on matrix regression with fixed-rank objectives and a specific range of positive definite objectives, as well as the standard restricted strong convexity landscape for low-rank matrix optimization, thereby providing a unified global view of the landscape for factorized objectives under fixed rank and PSD constraints. Finally, we outline several potential future extensions. Our contributions advance the current state of art by establishing a novel definition of restricted strong convexity and a corresponding restricted geodesic convexity, and by developing a comprehensive framework to analyze the restricted strong convexity landscape within search spaces governed by geodesic distances.

It has been established that if a graph $G$ has a maximum degree $\Delta(G) \leq 3$ and contains no isolated edges, then $\chi'_s(G) \leq 9$. In this note, we demonstrate that for each integer $k \geq 1$, there exists a graph $G_k$ with $\Delta(G_k) = 3$ such that $\chi'_s(G_k) \geq 2k+3$. Furthermore, we prove that every graph $G$ with $\Delta(G) \leq 3$ and no isolated edges satisfies $\chi'_s(G) \leq 2\Delta(G)+1$. Consequently, the strongest possible upper bound for a graph $G$ with $\Delta(G) \leq 3$ and no isolated edges is $\chi'_s(G) \leq 7$. Consequently, for each integer $k \geq 1$, there exists a graph $G_k$ with $\Delta(G_k) = 3$ such that $\chi'_s(G_k) \geq 2k+3$. Additionally, we establish that a list strong edge-coloring exists for any graph $G$ with $\Delta(G) \leq 3$ and no isolated edges when assigned a set of two distinct colors for each edge. These findings generalize previous work by Wang and Li (2019) and Hu (2015). 2010 Mathematics Subject Classification: 05C15, 05C30.

Our introduced "social-learning" variants successfully establish this equilibrium, whereas "individual learning" versions fail to converge strategies to the Nash outcome. When players utilize "canonical co-evolutionary genetic algorithms," the game dynamics form an ergodic Markov Chain; consequently, we analyze simulation results using both specific methodologies and broader statistical tests. We also estimate the time required for "social" algorithms to reach the "NE state," verify their robustness, and demonstrate that a substantial proportion of played games indeed occur at the Nash Equilibrium. To ensure reliability in real-world deployments, these systems must remain robust against hardware soft errors that corrupt platform memory. Building on the proven effectiveness of activation clipping, this study constructs a preliminary safety case for classifier CNNs by showing that range supervision acts as a highly dependable fault detector and mitigator for relevant bit flips, specifically within an eight-exponent floating-point format. Additionally, we investigate novel, non-uniform range restriction techniques that successfully reduce the likelihood of silent data corruptions and uncorrectable errors. As a practical, safety-critical end-to-end demonstration, we apply our method to a vehicle classification task using ResNet-50 and the MIOVision traffic camera dataset. The quantitative results presented here can serve as a foundation for developing further, potentially more sophisticated, safety arguments for CNNs. To support this effort, we open-source a readily usable Python implementation of our approach. Furthermore, we provide access to an extensive collection of high-performance Python scripts designed for large-scale, fault injection testing of deep neural networks on supercomputers. Our findings indicate that, in a standard scenario involving a mainstream eight-exponent floating-point format, the scene classification problem exhibits an approximate 10x safety margin against random, single, relevant bit flips. However, we also note that the presence of long tails of unlikely, multi-word errors suggests that a truly 100% safe system of uptime would require error correction codes (ECC). To facilitate future, more rigorous safety case developments, we release a structured dataset containing the essential elements required for quantitative analysis, including the code for bit error injection, detailed statistics, and reliability calculations.

Extending beyond simple word alignment, we implement multiple cluster-level alignments, ensuring that word clusters maintain consistent positions across the semantic space. This approach leverages cluster-level alignments to restore or enhance the bilateral or multilateral clustering structure of related words within each language's vocabulary. Our results indicate that this method yields substantial trilingual improvements, particularly in vocabulary enrichment scenarios where we restore bisentential clusters from a third language using only sparse, dense, and implicit resources. We present a comprehensive guide to constructing such common semantic spaces, detailing the process of iterative cluster-level alignment and the optimization of an objective function that balances distributional semantics with cluster-level alignment. Comparative analyses demonstrate that this approach outperforms other cross-lingual alignment techniques, offering significant benefits for few-shot and even zero-shot vocabulary enrichment. Furthermore, we release a trilingual common semantic space for Romanian, Portuguese, and Spanish, which can be utilized for diverse NLP tasks requiring cross-lingual knowledge transfer. Cross-lingual evaluation confirms that models trained on monolingual data and leveraging this common semantic space achieve performance boosts, especially in zero-shot and few-shot settings. Furthermore, we observe that making cluster-level alignments implicit rather than explicit leads to better performance, and we provide comparative analyses of clustering mechanisms used within each language's vocabulary. Our findings suggest that common semantic spaces, even when relying solely on sparse, implicit, and indirect resources, effectively organize and share cross-lingual knowledge, particularly vocabulary, across multiple languages. Consequently, such spaces are invaluable for optimizing NLP applications that involve vocabulary enrichment from languages with limited resources. We conclude by suggesting potential extensions to tasks involving more complex cross-lingual knowledge sharing, such as sentential and document-level applications.

Relativistic heavy-ion collisions serve as a unique environment for probing the properties of matter at extreme energy and density conditions. The creation of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP)—the state of matter with the highest energy and density—can be inferred from the collective flow of emitted particles and the particle species produced. Additionally, the chemical composition of final-state particles provides critical insights into the thermodynamic parameters of the system. Consequently, data from the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) are essential for advancing our understanding of hadron chemistry and thermalization in intermediate-sized nuclei. Previous analyses of particle production in lead-lead collisions at $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 2.76$ and 1.23 TeV have demonstrated that certain particle ratios, such as kaon-to-pion and proton-to-pion, align with statistical model predictions only at the highest charged-particle multiplicities \[@Abe09,\ @Abe10,\ @Abe11,\ @Abe12,\ @Abe13,\ @Abe14,\ @Abe15,\ @Abe16,\ @Abe18,\ @Abe19,\ @Abe20,\ @Abe21

9, Chile, particularly its capital Santiago, experienced extensive violence that resulted in the destruction of both public and private infrastructure. This study seeks to extend an epidemiological non-local model, previously effective in describing the 2005 French riots, to include the topological structure of Santiago's subway network and account for the observed spatial distribution of rioting. While the model accurately replicated the aggregated temporal progression of the disorders, it failed to reproduce the actual spatial pattern of activity in Santiago. This discrepancy is primarily due to the model's absence of a population displacement mechanism, a factor deemed essential for explaining the unrest episodes in the city. While such a mechanism was indeed present and critical in the riots of Paris in 2005, it was not identified as a driver of spatial distribution in the challenges related to the Chilean incidents. Consequently, incorporating population displacement into the model offers a potential route to accounting for the spatial dynamics of riots, thereby enhancing the overall representation of violent episodes along a city's transit network. This case study underscores the necessity of aligning model features with the specific characteristics of each set of riots to ensure accurate explanations of their spatial behaviors. Ensuring that displacement remains a key feature in such explanations is vital for developing effective strategies to mitigate future outbreaks of civil unrest. Ensuring resource allocation along transit networks remains a potential area for triggering future riots, yet integrating population displacement into relevant models is essential for correctly explaining any resulting disturbances. The current study indicates that the rapid, concentrated destruction of infrastructure in Santiago, especially in central areas, can be explained by a mechanism involving population funnelling and displacement within the city.

Unlike standard methods that fail to address extended operators or infinite alphabets, the proposed algorithm bypasses the conversion to equivalent automata. Instead, it employs a purely symbolic term rewriting system to resolve regular expression inequalities. . Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) leverages data from cameras and inertial sensors to determine position and orientation. Recently, deep learning-based VIO approaches have gained significant interest because they derive pose information through data-driven methods, eliminating the need for manually designed algorithms. However, current learning-based VIO systems typically depend on recurrent models to integrate multimodal data and process sensor signals, which often struggle with training difficulties and lack sufficient efficiency. We introduce a novel learning-based VIO framework utilizing external memory attention, which effectively and efficiently fuses visual and inertial features for state estimation. This proposed model achieves accurate and robust pose estimation, even in challenging conditions such as overcast days and water-covered terrain—scenarios where traditional VIO algorithms fail to extract visual features. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach surpasses both conventional and existing learning-based VIO baselines across various scenes. Additionally, comparisons with internal attention models reveal the significance of directly incorporating prior inertial information. Finally, we note that the mentioned dataset remains inaccessible to the public, and our source code is also unavailable.

This Letter introduces a square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal (SHOWS) model by adapting characteristics from its parent Hamiltonians. Our findings reveal that SHOWS supports both "Fermi-arc" surface states and hinge states linking the projections of Weyl points. We successfully constructed this exotic SHOWS state theoretically and observed it experimentally in three-dimensional (3D) stacked electric circuits featuring honeycomb-kagome hybridizations and double-helix interlayer couplings. These results pave the way for achieving square-root topology within 3D solid-state systems.

Semimetals defined by the intersection of quadratic bands are currently a major focus of condensed-matter research. However, defining and observing "square-root topology"—where square-root Hamiltonians possess features typical of Weyl semimetals, such as surface arcs and hinge states—is challenging because their unitary limit typically yields trivial topology. We propose a proposal to realize SHOWS (square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal) experimentally in 3D stacked electric circuits. The necessary double-helix capacitors are feasible with current technology, and our design is based on a theoretical framework applicable to any 3D lattice. This results in SHOWS within a 4-layer honeycomb-kagome-honeycomb-honeycomb network, characterized by finite surface arcs and hinge states at frequencies distinct from each other and from the band edges. This system can be built with feasible components, as the double-helix capacitor can be replaced by a series combination of two standard capacitors. Our work provides a theoretical framework for identifying and constructing SHOWS in other square-root models.

FedSA), a novel knowledge-amalgamation problem aimed at training a student model for a specific new task using multiple decentralized teacher models. These teachers possess pre-training tasks and datasets that are distinct and mutually unknown. Our motivation arises from a current challenge in model sharing: despite significant investments in training large, capable networks, researchers and institutions often cannot share their pre-trained models due to privacy, security, or intellectual property concerns, even when they wish to contribute. FedSA addresses this dilemma by enabling the creation of a specialized student model for a task different from any of the teachers' original domains. To achieve this, we propose a dedicated strategy where the student training process employs a new saliency-based method to adaptively select participating teachers and integrate their key capabilities. We evaluate FedSA's effectiveness across both single-task and multi-task scenarios. The experimental results confirm that FedSA successfully amalgamates knowledge from decentralized models, achieving performance competitive with centralized baselines.

To better understand the quantum thermodynamics of many-body systems, we investigate whether the QNEC constrains irreversible entropy production during quenches driven by energy-momentum inflow from an infinite memoryless bath within two-dimensional holographic theories. Our findings indicate that while the increase in both entropy and temperature—mandated by the Clausius inequality of classical thermodynamics—is necessary to avoid violating the QNEC in quenches involving transitions between thermal states with momentum (dual to BTZ geometries), it is not sufficient. For any initial state, we establish analytic lower and upper bounds on the entropy production of thermal states under the assumption of conformal invariance; these bounds intersect at the critical temperature defined by the phase transition between conformal and thermal phases. Furthermore, we numerically determine the actual irreversible entropy production for various boosts applied to thermal states and observe that it lies between the established lower and upper bounds. To facilitate this, we derived the analytic entanglement entropy of the thermal state prior to the quenches. Our results demonstrate that the QNEC provides meaningful insights into the irreversibility of quantum thermodynamic processes and define precise bounds for entropy production following perturbations by Riemannian metrics. The study relies on recently developed computational methods for calculating entanglement entropy and entropy current within the context of the quantum entanglement/hope duality. This work extends our earlier research on understanding thermodynamic irreversibility and the significance of the QNEC through the holographic principle.

quantum computing. To bring this technology to practical viability, it is essential to detect and mitigate material defects that cause decoherence. In this study, we employ terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy (SNOM) to examine the local dielectric characteristics and carrier densities of wet-etched aluminum resonators on silicon, a fundamental component of superconducting quantum processors. Leveraging a newly developed vector calibration method, we derive THz permittivity from spectroscopy conducted near the plasma frequency of silicon. By comparing our THz-derived results with existing data across frequencies, temperatures, and environments, we offer quantitative insights into near-surface phenomena, including silicon carrier density, two-level system (TLS) modes, and their interaction with electrons. Our findings indicate that in resonators exhibiting high two-level system losses, a substantial population of TLSs resides within the etched regions near the aluminum-dielectric interface. However, in low-loss devices, many of these TLSs are located deeper within the dielectric layer. Furthermore, we demonstrate that TNR etching significantly reduces surface carrier densities and associated TLS losses compared to standard Bosch etching. We conclude by discussing the implications of our findings for fabricating higher-performance quantum circuits. TNR: Two-Nanometer-Removal.

and how its composition is modulated by interactions between the planet's interior and exterior. The processes that formed and evolved Venus's atmosphere to its current surface conditions remain subjects of intense debate, encompassing questions that span multiple disciplines. We investigate these interconnected mechanisms, beginning with volatile sources and sinks, and trace the path from the deep interior to the upper atmosphere, covering volcanic outgassing, surface-atmosphere interactions, and atmospheric escape. Additionally, we address complex historical factors, such as the impact of Late Accretion events, the connection between magnetic field generation and long-term evolution, and the effects of geochemical and geodynamical feedback cycles on the atmosphere. Based on modeling and observations, we outline plausible evolutionary pathways for Venus from accretion to its present state. Three specific scenarios are highlighted: first, desiccation caused by atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase; second, a prolonged period of surface liquid water followed by climate destabilization and a runaway greenhouse effect; and third, inefficient outgassing that retained water within the planet, trapping hydrogen in the core and oxidizing the mantle. Finally, we discuss current evidence and the future observations and missions needed to refine our understanding of Venus's history and the intricate feedback cycles operating among its interior, surface, and atmosphere across past, present, and future timescales.

Among these, the Hawkes process is particularly popular due to its ability to define the probability of new events based on the process's history. This study focuses on the nonlinear Hawkes process, which effectively captures excitation and inhibition dynamics between different dimensions. Within a nonparametric Bayesian estimation framework, we derive concentration rates for the posterior distribution regarding the parameters, assuming only mild conditions on the prior and the model. These findings also establish convergence rates for Bayesian estimators. Additionally, a key aspect of event-data modeling is reconstructing the interaction graph, or Granger connectivity graph. We demonstrate consistency guarantees for Bayesian approaches in estimating this structure, specifically proving that the posterior distribution remains consistent for the process's graph adjacency matrix and that a Bayesian estimator using a suitable loss function achieves consistency. Where applicable, our results improve upon existing consistency rates found in literature. Finally, the proposed methods are applied to real-world data consisting of geological earthquakes and Twitter communications regarding the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear disaster.

Bayesian inference offers a robust framework for estimating parameters of multivariate Hawkes processes, yielding consistent results when appropriate loss functions are used. This paper enhances previous consistency guarantees for such Bayesian estimators and extends findings to the case where the process dimension grows at a rate relative to the available data. Furthermore, we address the estimation of the Granger connectivity graph representing interactions within the process. While past research has established conditions for a Bayesian estimator's validity and the consistency of its parameters, we prove that a necessary condition for this estimator to consistently recover the true graph (assuming it is known a priori) is also sufficient for the process dimension to be consistent. Regarding a "plug-in" estimator for the same task, we demonstrate consistency assuming the process dimension is consistent. Additionally, we investigate the complexity of the parameter space's likelihood level sets to confirm the stability of the Bayesian estimator's consistency. The analysis includes both continuous and discrete-type multivariate Hawkes processes, with results extended to scenarios where the dimension is increasing with data size; in this context, we establish consistency for a "rolling window" estimator. All proposed estimators demonstrate performance in sim studies and on real earthquake data. Our code is publicly available on GitHub. (The source code is also accessible within the published article.)

We introduce a plasma waveplate utilizing magneto-optical birefringence under a transverse magnetic field, designed to operate under ultra-high peak power conditions. Uniquely, this device not only modifies the polarization state but also amplifies the input laser pulse under optimized conditions, acting similarly to an optical isolator. Numerical simulations demonstrate that a waveplate operating at terawatt-level peak powers (corresponding to ~1014 W/cm2 intensity) is feasible with current technology, featuring a 1mm thickness and a 0.5T magnetic field strength. Furthermore, this plasma waveplate is intrinsically an optical isolator, offering substantial amplitude transmission while completely blocking reverse-direction propagation under the same conditions, thus eliminating the need for separate isolators in laser systems. This plasma-based solution provides all-necessary conditions for polarizing and isolating petawatt-laser beams, as it remains functional across the entire intensity range, from low powers where the plasma remains under-dense to high powers approaching relativistic laser intensities. Key material and simulation results validate the feasible design parameters. This innovation represents a major breakthrough in polarizing petawatt-laser beams, addressing a longstanding challenge in high-intensity laser physics that has thus far lacked an established solution. The proposed plasma waveplate holds significant potential for diverse applications, including self-amplification of high-power pulses, the development of optical isolators, signal modulation, and the generation of circular/polarized petawatt-laser beams. This plasma-based approach represents a pioneering and cost-effective solution for polarizing and isolating petawatt-class laser beams.

We outline the general framework of optimal observables and apply it to two $CP$-odd quantities sensitive to the real and imaginary components of $d_\tau(s)$, respectively. Full kinematic information is utilized for $\tau$ decays involving two pions or three charged pions. Under the assumption that the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator will eventually process data with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$, and applying acceptance cuts on final-state pions, we determine that 1~s.d. sensitivities of $\delta {\rm Re} d_\tau = 6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $\delta {\rm} Im d_\tau = 4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm can be achieved. Consequently, we conclude that the optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau^+ \tau^-$ production at Belle II are capable of tightening the constraints on the real and imaginary parts of the tau electric dipole form factor by roughly a factor of ten compared to current limits. The tabulated results for optimal $CP$ observables will prove valuable for analyzing the increasingly precise data expected from the Belle II experiment.

We find that when these blocks are constructed from conserved spinning primaries, the integral decomposes into a product of two weighted AdS$_{2}$ field copies, smeared along geodesics. Consequently, conserved current OPE blocks in CFT$_{2}$ admit a distinct formulation via AdS$_{2}$ geodesic operators rather than the traditional AdS$_{3}$ geodesic operators. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this perspective connects to AdS$_{3}$ massless higher spin fields through HKLL bulk field reconstruction. Leveraging this framework, we successfully derive a closed-form expression for the four-point spinning conformal block as a product of two AdS$_{2}$ Geodesic Witten diagrams. Additionally, we establish a novel integral representation for four-point spinning conformal blocks by combining an existing expression for AdS$_{2}$ massless higher spin field reconstruction with the Geodesic AdS$_{3}$ OPE block formulation. In the large spin limit, our method yields a consistent and expected result: a single AdS$_{3}$ field copy represented as an integral over two AdS$_{2}$ field copies. Consequently, our proposed integral representation holds significance not only for AdS$_{3}$ / CFT$_{2}$ gravity dualities but also for understanding massless higher spin gravity within AdS$_{3}$. To our knowledge, this represents the first instance of a closed-form expression for four-point spinning conformal blocks, aside from recent findings in \cite{Chen:2021qai}. Our approach involves training a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on the initial snapshots of a dark matter-only simulation to forecast the halo mass into which individual particles will collapse by $z=0$, within the range $10.5 < \log(M / M_{\odot}) < 14$. This adjustment allowed us to observe velocity impacts on larger halos that fall within our simulation's resolution. Consequently, the CNN model trained on simulations with a higher $A_s$ demonstrated significant improvements in halo mass prediction when velocity field data were included. Ultimately, for simulations where $A_s = 8 \times 10^{-9}$, the model relying solely on density information exhibited at least an $80\%$ increase in mean squared error compared to the model utilizing both velocity and density across nearly all mass scales, highlighting the failure of the density-only approach in this scenario. Designed with quasi-static evolutionary applications in mind, our method utilizes a custom-developed Lagrangian formulation. Unlike the standard Eulerian approach, this formulation solves force balance equations to determine the positions of fluid elements mapped to grid points. Distinct from prior literature, we do not rely on the first integral of the Euler equation, which typically lacks a general analytic solution. Instead of prescribing the spatial distribution of angular velocity or angular momentum as previous methods do, we assign specific mass, angular momentum, and entropy to each fluid element; the angular velocity and momentum distributions are subsequently derived once the positions of all elements are established. We discretize the time-independent Euler and Einstein equations using the finite-element method, resulting in a large system of nonlinear algebraic equations that we solve via our new multi-dimensional root-finding algorithm, the W4 method. To validate this formulation, we have constructed both barotropic and baroclinic rotational configurations and solved three evolutionary sequences that simulate cooling, mass loss, and mass accretion as simplified toy models. Our results indicate that these new baroclinic configurations serve as an extremely stable initial value for the Einstein and Einstein solver suites, including those from \texttt{RATTAIL} and \texttt{ROST}. Furthermore, the algorithm automatically preserves the conservation of mass, angular momentum, and entropy throughout the calculation. We have made the code publicly accessible at https://www.eqstar.astr.s.u-tokyo.ac.jp/. The final paragraph of this paper outlines the algorithmic procedure for computing evolutionary paths of compact objects, such as double stars and accretion disks.

For events involving neutron stars, the concurrent detection of gravitational and electromagnetic radiation offers significant potential to deepen our understanding of these phenomena and investigate the equation of state of dense matter. However, achieving electromagnetic follow-up for gravitational wave (GW) events demands rapid, real-time signal detection and classification, a task where traditional methods are too computationally demanding for the expected detection rates of next-generation instruments. Specifically, we trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) on approximately 500,000 real LIGO noise samples containing injected BBH, BNS, and NSBH signals, achieving high sensitivity and accuracy. These findings represent a substantial advancement over prior studies, which were limited to analyzing simulated data. Furthermore, we provide suggestions for optimizing future classification efforts targeting second-generation detectors. The code employed in this research is accessible on GitHub.

This study examines shifts in the income diversity of urban interactions across various pandemic phases, leveraging a privacy-preserving dataset of over one million anonymized mobile phone users from four major U.S. cities, spanning three years before and during the crisis. These encounters occur in diverse settings, including workplaces, public transit, restaurants, and recreational areas. This paper introduces and measures "Urban Encounter Diversity" (UED), utilizing anonymized aggregated mobile location data to track changes in the variety of urban physical meetings before, during, and after the COVID-19 pandemic in four large U.S. cities (Atlanta, Baltimore, Chicago, and Houston). Our analysis of nine years of data demonstrates that UED decreased substantially at every data granularity level during the pandemic's initial phases and remained significantly lower than pre-pandemic levels as of late 2021, despite aggregate mobility figures in these cities having reverted to baseline. These findings align with observations of diminished social media interaction diversity during the pandemic. Furthermore, our counterfactual analysis reveals that the suppression of UED was driven not only by behavioral changes, such as increased time spent at home and reduced willingness to visit new places, but also by shifts in the location choice functions of urbanites, indicating potential permanent alterations to urban activity patterns. These results underscore the need for careful consideration of the impact of COVID-19 policies on the diversity of urban encounters when designing the path forward post-pandemic.

-mass young stellar objects (HMYSOs) often fragment into multiple self-gravitating bodies, a process that may account for recently observed episodic accretion bursts. By applying a 1D code to resolve dynamics down to the stellar surface, we post-processed prior 3D simulation results. Our findings reveal that the burst-like deposition of material into the inner disc observed in 3D models does not invariably produce powerful accretion bursts; instead, only fragments with sufficiently high specific angular momentum and internal pressure succeed in reaching the stars. While some fragments do exhibit burst-like accretion episodes, others accumulate in the inner disc and release energy through thermal (viscous) processes over longer timescales. These results underscore the necessity of high-resolution modeling that encompasses both the fragments and the inner disc to fully understand the physics of HMYSO outflows. Such models confirm that accretion from fragments can indeed trigger episodic bursts, but only under specific conditions. We present a simple criterion based on the Toomre parameter and the ratio of Keplerian to total specific energy to identify which fragments will produce bursts in future simulations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the mass of these bursting fragments can remain below the detection limits of current interferometric observations.

The primary objective is to characterize how uniform shear flow influences the modulation of weakly nonlinear, quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves. By employing Hamiltonian transformation theory on the Hamiltonian formulation of the system, we derive a Hamiltonian Dysthe equation governing the temporal evolution of the wave envelope. Consistent with prior findings, our results indicate that the impact of uniform shear flow on the modulational instability of Stokes waves is contingent upon the vorticity profile. Specifically, we identify two distinct flow regimes: one where the maximum vorticity $\zeta_{\text{max}}$ is less than $2\pi$ and another where $\zeta_{\text{max}}$ exceeds $2\pi$. In the former regime, the instability growth rate is reduced, whereas in the latter, it is enhanced. Furthermore, our approach successfully recovers the Dysthe equation for the zero-vorticity scenario, thereby establishing an explicit expression for the modification of the Dysthe matrix by a nonzero uniform shear flow. These theoretical conclusions are validated against direct numerical simulations. The significance of these findings lies in their quantification of the intricate dynamics arising from the interaction between nonlinear quasi-monochromatic surface gravity waves and constant rotational shear flow. This methodology offers a structured framework for analyzing Hamiltonian Dysthe equations and their associated Dysthe matrices in varying current scenarios. Additionally, the results demonstrate that the influence of non-uniform current profiles on the instability of weakly nonlinear surface waves is not merely a direct extension of uniform flow effects; rather, the complexity increases as higher amplitudes of vertical shear are incorporated. Our findings align with and extend previous studies by Dysthe and Mueller (J. Fluid Mech. **845**, 825, 2018) and Grue and Krogstad (arXiv:1906.00505, 2019). The derived expressions for the Dysthe matrix under uniform shear flow can be applied to determine critical current thresholds and the growth rate of the instability for any arbitrary vertical profile, a outcome that contradicts simplistic predictions based on the principle of superposition. Ultimately, this work underscores the necessity of solving the Dysthe system directly when dealing with strongly varying current profiles, as approximate models based on uniform shear flow assumptions may yield inaccurate or misleading results.

This paper introduces a solution that leverages transformer-based language models while mitigating a key limitation inherent to them. Additionally, we present an open-source implementation available at this GitHub repository: https://github.com/erincetinkol/CMTR-BERT. The proposed framework serves as a robust, state-of-the-art framework for assessing fake news, surpassing existing approaches by leveraging multi-modal representations and contextual awareness. Comprehensive experimental results confirm these claims, demonstrating significant performance improvements over baseline models. Furthermore, this research contributes to the literature by introducing a summarization-based methodology for fake news detection that synergistically combines various representation types and contextual cues. Consequently, the CMTR-BERT framework represents a cutting-edge approach to this challenge, utilizing contextualized deep learning techniques with textual data that encapsulates semantic and syntactic nuances. This work also addresses a significant gap in current literature regarding the incorporation of contextual information into fake news assessment. Ultimately, the CMTR-BERT framework represents a robust, state-of-the-art framework for evaluating deceptive content. This study employs multiple datasets to validate the effectiveness of our method, showcasing its potential for real-world deployment and providing a resource for future researchers. By applying Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods, we simulate the evolution of these fields to determine the Gaussian curvature of the parametric space, examining its behavior across phase transitions. $\ell_1$-norm principal component analysis (L1-PCA), a robust alternative to conventional PCA, has gained significant popularity in recent years. This study examines a rotationally invariant variant of L1-PCA, which remains largely unexplored in existing literature. To address this challenge, we introduce a proximal alternating linearized minimization method incorporating nonlinear extrapolation to solve the problem's equivalent quadratic formulation. We further demonstrate that the proposed algorithm converges at least linearly to a stationary point. Numerical experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world datasets validates the numerical validity of our findings. Key contributions of this paper include: (i) addressing a previously uninvestigated problem type, and (ii) providing a robust solution to L1-PCA that is capable of handling outlier-contaminated data.

In this study, we introduce a new dataset comprising approximately 2000 paraphrases of "Emotion Twenty Questions" (EMO20Q) utterances. We develop a method to fine-tune a BERT neural network to compare the semantic similarity of EMO20Q statements. In this study, we introduce a Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry setup designed to measure extremely weak local magnetic fields expelled by a superconductor—acting as a "testing magnet"—via the Meissner effect. The resulting magnetic field gradient near the superconductor generates a centripetal acceleration on the atoms within the interferometer, enabling detection through atomic interference patterns. Building on the fact that gravitational acceleration of atoms has been measured with a precision of $10^{-12}$ g, the sensitivity of this method for detecting the expelled local field could potentially achieve $10^{-14}$ T. However, if the superconductor is coated with a normal metal, the expelled magnetic field can approach the material's intrinsic magnetic susceptibility, which is approximately two orders of magnitude higher than the Meissner effect. Consequently, this "testing magnet" is sufficiently strong to enable high-precision magnetometry while simultaneously serving to calibrate errors arising from the skin effect. Consequently, this Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry technique offers a simple yet highly precise method for detecting and measuring the expulsion of magnetic fields by superconductors, making it particularly valuable for evaluating the magnetic performance of next-generation low-loss superconducting magnets used in large-scale facilities such as the Superconducting Linear Accelerator (SLAC), the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), and the International Linear Collider (ILC). To demonstrate the feasibility of this detection method, a proof-of-principle experiment using the Earth's magnetic field was recently implemented at our laboratory. The experimental setup and data analysis methods can be readily adapted to detect and quantify the magnetic field expelled by any superconducting sample. This approach complements existing magnetic measurement tools, such as SQUID magnetometers and Hall probes, by offering superior long-term stability and higher magnetic field sensitivity. Furthermore, the experiment can be quickly modified to assess the actual operating conditions of large-scale superconducting installations, addressing limitations caused by environmental noise and measurement uncertainties inherent in traditional methods. Beyond its immediate utility, this setup provides a means to monitor the long-term stability of laboratory magnetic environments and to calibrate minor uncertainties in other magnetometry techniques. The detection of magnetic fields expelled by superconductors through this method represents a direct manifestation of the Meissner effect, distinct from manifestations related to the skin effect. Therefore, this technique is especially well-suited for validating samples of new testing magnets that may suffer from errors due to the skin effect, including those currently being commissioned at major facilities like SLAC,

We have identified a broad category of object-oriented programs, including many significant real-world applications, that can be efficiently executed on massively parallel SIMD accelerators. We term this category Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), as it expresses parallelism by executing a specific method across all instances of a given type.

To enable average programmers to utilize fast GPU programming for SMMO applications, we developed DynaSOAr, a CUDA framework. DynaSOAr comprises three core components: (1) a fully parallel, lock-free, dynamic memory allocator; (2) a data layout Domain-Specific Language (DSL); and (3) an efficient, parallel do-all operation. By controlling both memory allocation and access, DynaSOAr outperforms state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators.

DynaSOAr enhances memory utilization by adopting a Structure of Arrays (SoA) data layout and reduces memory fragmentation through the efficient management of free and allocated blocks using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps. Unlike other allocators, our design relies heavily on atomic operations, prioritizing overall application performance over individual method execution speed.

To ensure coalesced memory access, DynaSOAr maps a method call on all object instances to a data-parallel do-all operation. This operation iterates over contiguous, equal-sized memory blocks where each block holds the data for a single object. Consequently, any read or write to the $i$-th object targets a specific, pre-calculated offset within that object's dedicated memory block.

In terms of data layout, DynaSOAr adopts an SoA approach, storing each object's attributes in separate, contiguous memory blocks. While this may seem counterintuitive for cache coherence, our benchmarks show it rarely causes a performance penalty. We manage memory allocation and access efficiently using lock-free, hierarchical bitmaps, avoiding the need to atomically allocate individual elements as in other allocators. Instead, we atomically allocate entire blocks of consecutive elements, leveraging the fact that objects of the same type usually have identical sizes.

Our evaluation indicates that DynaSOAr matches the throughput of manual CUDA programming for a representative SMMO benchmark and surpasses the direct use

Additionally, we introduce a general method for constructing irreducible graphs, utilizing which we define a specific family of "new" irreducible graphs that have densities exactly equal to our proposed bound. These new irreducible graphs are situated within the interval $(1-\sqrt{1-\frac{4}{p+3}}, 1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{p+3}}]$ for every prime $p \geq 7$. set $S \subseteq G$, the diameter $diam(G,S)$ denotes the smallest integer $n$ such that every element of $G$ can be expressed as a product of at most $n$ elements from $S$. In this work, assuming $|S|$ is bounded, we identify groups with polynomial diameter as those possessing a substantial abelian section near the top, specifically one whose size constitutes an exponential fraction of the total group order. This finding extends a significant result by Breuillard and Tointon. Consequently, groups exhibiting polynomial diameter are shown to contain a large nilpotent subgroup of class at most $2$ and to possess a high number of conjugacy classes. These results generalize a theorem by [Guralnick and Mazur, 1997]. Our primary tool is a recent framework by [Breuillard, 2010] that utilizes a graph associated with the group to extend the analysis found in [Breuillard and Tointon, 2012]. Regarding converse statements, we observe that large abelian sections are not necessarily required for polynomial diameter, as infinite groups satisfying this condition include $F_g \times Z_2$ and ${Z_2}^G$ for any $g \geq 1$ and infinite set $G$, where $F_g$ represents the free group on $g$ generators. Furthermore, we provide an infinite family of groups with polynomial diameter that contain a large section isomorphic to $A_n$ for sufficiently large $n$. Finally, we establish an upper bound of $O_p(d^k)$ for the number of conjugacy classes in groups where the diameter is at most $d$ and $|S|$ is no greater than $k$, improving upon a result by [Aschbacher, 1984] which stated $O_d(|G|^{1-\epsilon})$. Notably, since the exponent of the polynomial in our theorem is not explicitly defined, our approach offers a significantly sharper bound compared to [Aschbacher, 1984].

The sensor's front-end utilizes a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to transform local temperature into two biasing currents, which subsequently determine two oscillation frequencies. The ratio of these frequencies corresponds directly to the absolute temperature. The back-end then converts this frequency ratio into a digital temperature code. Benefiting from its low-complexity architecture, the design offers a compact footprint, low power usage, and high accuracy across a broad temperature spectrum. Additionally, an embedded line regulation mechanism enables voltage scalability. Prototyped in 180nm CMOS, the sensor operates within a 0°C to 100°C detection range, supports a supply voltage from 0.6V to 1.8V, and occupies a minimal silicon area of 0.021mm². Experimental results from 20 test chips demonstrate competitive performance metrics, including a resolution of 0.24°C, an inaccuracy of ±1.4°C, a sampling rate of approximately 1.5kHz, and an energy consumption of 1.06nJ per conversion at 30°C. Furthermore, a mathematical model was developed to validate the sensor's linear behavior within a defined operating region and to facilitate the optimization of circuit parameters for customized specifications.

Statistical tests reveal that protostellar cores possess greater mass than starless cores, even when accounting for biases related to temperature and opacity. We propose that this mass disparity signifies core growth occurring after formation. Consequently, massive star formation may not necessarily originate from massive prestellar cores, contingent upon the rate of this mass accretion. The implications of this finding for the relationship between the core mass function and the stellar initial mass function require further investigation. Furthermore, core mass accretion could help resolve the observed excess of massive stars in various environments. Accretion continues post-formation; therefore, the masses of forming stars within this region may differ significantly from current estimates of the stellar initial mass function. If core accretion is universal, the properties of the highest-mass stars could be entirely determined by processes occurring after their initial formation. Future observations aimed at measuring core masses across a range of dark clouds are essential to generalize these conclusions.

We analyze both inextensible and highly extensible membranes, detailing the influence of membrane tension in each scenario. When the inner fluid is denser than the outer fluid, both systems display a centrifugally induced Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability that competes with restoring forces from curvature and tension, ultimately determining the finger scale. Numerical continuation methods are employed to calculate strongly nonlinear primary finger states up to self-contact, as well as secondary branches involving mixed modes and circumferentially localized folds, varying with rotation rate and external pressure. The analysis includes both reflection-symmetric and symmetry-broken chiral configurations, with results illustrated through bifurcation diagrams. Furthermore, the ratio of the system scale to the natural length scale is identified as the key factor governing the sequence of primary bifurcations from the unperturbed circular state, as well as the resulting solution profiles and the initiation of secondary bifurcations. The findings are interpreted using physical scaling arguments. The results indicate that, driven by centrifugal forces, extensible membranes generate larger fingers than those that are not. However, the spectral characteristics of the instability are solely determined by the system's geometric scaling, irrespective of whether the membrane is extensible. This work expands prior research on stationary, gravity-driven membranes by exploring the rich phenomenology of real, elastic membranes in rotating systems and offers insights for experimental validation. This model system provides valuable qualitative and quantitative observations on the competition between multiple restoring forces and centrifugal forces in elastic interfaces, yielding results relevant to various natural and industrial contexts, including planar solar wind pinch effects, black hole accretion disk phenomena, and agitated beverage foams.

Abramson and Parashar contend that a comparable divide exists between sophisticated computational technologies and increasingly demanding applications, necessitating a parallel field known as translational computer science. In this discipline, the intentional transition of research findings into large-scale practice becomes a primary research objective rather than a secondary consideration. This approach addresses the challenge of applying cutting-edge technology at massive scales.
