**I. Introduction**

The accelerating expansion of the universe remains a pivotal yet unresolved challenge in modern cosmology. Since the late 1990s, observations of high-redshift Type Ia supernovae [1–3] have indicated that the universe's expansion is speeding up. To explain this phenomenon, the most accepted solution involves a novel component known as dark energy (DE), which constitutes approximately 69% of the universe's energy density yet remains poorly understood [4–10]. The simplest and most studied theoretical representation is the $\Lambda$CDM model [11–20], where the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ corresponds to vacuum energy with a constant equation of state (EoS) parameter $\omega_\Lambda = p_\Lambda/\rho_\Lambda = -1$. However, several issues persist regarding the cosmological constant, including its extreme smallness, lack of symmetry, non-renormalizability, inability to account for

ays into invisible particles constrain light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter (DM). Utilizing low-energy effective field theories (EFTs) to model general neutrino interactions and Dirac fermion DM coupled to charm quarks, we conduct likelihood fits for individual neutrino and DM operators featuring distinct Lorentz structures and photon spectra for the process $J/\psi\to \gamma+{\rm invisible}$. We derive limits on decay branching fractions across various neutrino and DM scenarios, converting these into lower bounds on new energy scales. The strongest constraints on the energy scale for neutrino and DM EFTs are found to be 12.8 GeV and 11.6 GeV, respectively. Additionally, the purely invisible decay $J/\psi\to {\rm invisible}$ offers complementary constraints on effective operators, with energy scale bounds exceeding 100 GeV for dipole operators. We also determine limits on the DM-nucleon scattering cross section based on $J/\psi$ data. These invisible decay measurements are sensitive to light DM masses that remain unprobed by current direct detection experiments. Furthermore, the future Super Tau Charm Factory is projected to improve these limits by two orders of magnitude after a one-year run. The paper also includes an introduction to the relevant physics and detailed calculations of production cross sections and energy spectra for the final-state photons. This work highlights that the STCF will significantly advance our understanding of light weakly interacting DM by leveraging the largest available $J/\psi$ datasets.

In this expression, $\phi(x,b) = \mathbb{P}(\text{L\'evy}(1/2,\kappa(x,b))<0)$, where the parameter $\kappa(x,b)$ is given by $\frac{\sqrt{1-x} b - \sqrt{1+x}}{\sqrt{1-x} b + \sqrt{1+x}}$. The coefficient $b=b_S \geq 0$ quantifies the asymptotic asymmetry between positive and negative excursions of the walk, taking the value $b_s=1$ when the increments are symmetric. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for $\kappa(x,b) \mapsto \text{L\'evy}(\cdot, \kappa(x,b))$. These findings generalize and correct earlier results by Pemantle and Peres (1994), showing that for symmetric walks ($b=1$), $p(t,x) \sim (1-x) t^{-1/2}$ for small $x$ and large $t$. Additionally, we provide numerical evidence supporting the proposed asymptotic behavior of $p(t,x)$ across various small values of $x$ and asymmetric walk parameters $b \neq 1$. As a byproduct, we determine the convergence rate to the arcsine law for the proportion of time an unbiased random walk spends positive. Our analysis relies on the continuous time branching process approximation, previously utilized by Shepp and Teshlauje (1978) for the case $x=0$.

coupled to a scalar field featuring a two-parameter Higgs-like self-interaction is reformulated using a Chern-Simons form associated with the algebra $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$. Depending on the sign of the self-interaction couplings, the components $g^{\pm}$ correspond to $so(2,1)$ or $so(3,1)$. The field equations are expressed as the field strength of this $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$ connection. Within this framework, black holes are constructed by ensuring the total field strength vanishes on the manifold $\R\times\cIRl_1$, which implies the local triviality of the associated Chern-Simons bundle. Due to the topological nature of the theory, these solutions are completely characterized by the Chern-Simons charges of the pure $g^{+}$ and $g^{-}$ Chern-Simons theories, which parametrize the moduli space of black hole solutions. Consequently, the known (A)dS black holes in three dimensions — including BTZ, Teitelboin-JT, and Sch\"{o}rken black holes — are recovered. Furthermore, within this formalism, we demonstrate the existence of a novel family of $\R\times\cIRl_1$ black holes termed JC black holes, which generalize the BTZ black hole. These JC black holes arise when $g^{+}$ is linked to $so(2,1)$ and $g^{-}$ to $so(3,1)$, or vice versa. The JC black hole family encompasses the BTZ black hole and is fully determined by two real positive parameters. Consequently, the JC black hole solution is stable and carries a charge linked to a universally defined operator. Additionally, the semi-classical limit of the JC black hole is examined, and it is concluded that the JC black hole possesses negative mass and thermodynamic behavior analogous to that of an ideal gas. Finally, the Chern-Simons formulation proves valuable for investigating black holes in higher-dimensional spacetimes constructed as triples $\M^{d} = \R\times\Sigma$.

The relationship between these two concepts can be defined by the equation: imperative algorithms equal proofs with cuts. This insight motivates a broader generalization of pseudocode, termed *logical pseudocodes*, which parallels natural deduction proofs within computability logic \cite{Jap03,Jap08}. In this system, every statement maps directly to a specific step in a natural deduction proof. Consequently, the primary advantage of logical pseudocodes over traditional pseudocode is the assurance that each statement adheres to correctness and safety relative to the initial specifications. Furthermore, this approach represents an extension of the computability logic web (\colw) that incorporates forward reasoning capabilities. The following sections detail the system's design and implementation, covering its various components and their development process. Ultimately, this work serves to introduce logical pseudocodes to the research community and provides instructions for executing them using the \texttt{cl-pdc} library on the \colw platform. Like the \colw, this library is open-source. The key innovation of this paper is the concept of logical pseudocodes themselves. While the implementation is original, it was facilitated by the CL_engine library and supporting tools created by the author and their colleagues at the Computer Science Department, Bar Ilan University. We hope that researchers and practitioners interested in the uniform integration of proofs and algorithms will find this approach both appealing and practical.

By segmenting the grid into superstates, such as "rooms," the method establishes a dual-resolution decision-making system comprising local PEGs at the granular state level and an aggregated PEG at the superstate level. Due to their reduced state space size, both the local and aggregated games can be efficiently solved to reach a Nash equilibrium. Focusing on muon colliders, we re-examine the validity of $W$ and $Z$ parton distribution functions (PDFs) at leading order for $2\to n$ processes. We systematically analyze universal and quasi-universal power-law and logarithmic corrections that emerge when deriving (polarized) weak boson PDFs in the collinear limit. Furthermore, we survey numerous $2\to n$ processes at center-of-mass energies ranging from 2 to 30 TeV through polarized and unpolarized electroweak boson fusion and scattering. To facilitate this, we present a public implementation of the Effective $W/Z$ and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations—collectively termed the Effective Vector Boson Approximation—within the Monte Carlo event generator \texttt{MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO}. This implementation establishes the foundation for creating matrix-element matching schemes that incorporate EW parton showers and renormalized EW PDFs. In support of this initiative, we conduct extensive investigations into the kinematic validity of the EW boson approximation, evaluate the magnitude of higher-order terms neglected in the collinear limit, and assess the resolution of final-state kinematics. Our results demonstrate that the effective approach yields precise results for observables that depend solely on the EW bosons' transverse momenta and radiation-less EW boson kinematics. However, this precision is not achieved for variables derived from the leptonic decay products of the EW bosons, unless specific radiative corrections are incorporated. These corrections include effects from final-state radiation, the polarization of radiating leptons, and kinematic smearing induced by the radiation of real or virtual EW bosons. While this paper lays the groundwork for utilizing effective EW PDFs and the effective AWB approximation in perturbative calculations for muon colliders, the considerations regarding radiative corrections to decay observables are broadly relevant to any lepton collider. These proofs share significant similarities and employ nearly identical techniques. Presenting them collectively offers a clearer and more intuitive understanding. Furthermore, this aggregation provides a robust foundation for teaching these classics, as all four proofs rely on the exact same underlying mechanism. The primary educational hurdle in instructing with these proofs lies not in their complexity, but in the difficult notation and terminology used by Godel and his contemporaries. To overcome this, we introduce a modern, accessible notation and reformulate the problems in a completionistic manner instead of the traditional diagonalizing approach. This allows us to represent the intricate proofs with remarkably concise code. Our methodology serves as a pivotal teaching tool, enabling readers to grasp the essence of these profound ideas without being overwhelmed by technical details. The underlying code is fully functional; beyond facilitating comprehension, it allows for the exploration of extensions to Godel's theorem, alternative proofs of Tarski's result, and variations of Rosser's theorem. The structured organization and contemporary notation of this article are specifically designed for use as a textbook. We aim to guide readers through the construction of these proofs step-by-step, utilizing guiding questions and explanations to ensure a thorough understanding. The code serves both to simplify the proofs and as an instructional aid, helping readers appreciate the elegance of these classical results. This article targets anyone capable of reading basic programming code in a non-deductive style. The causes of incompleteness are deep and multifaceted, impacting not only mathematics and logic but also computer science. Additionally, the code can be adapted to handle extended languages featuring decisive operators, such as random number generators. Our structured framework makes it straightforward to incorporate these or other modifications; we even include a sample implementation of an algorithm finding maximum array elements to illustrate this capability. of dynamical systems. This paper offers a concise overview of invariant sets, presenting findings on the existence of invariant lines and parabolas within planar polynomial systems. Additionally, we establish the criteria required for linear subspaces to remain invariant in fractional-order systems. Furthermore, we highlight a significant result demonstrating that, aside from linear subspaces, no other invariant manifolds exist in such fractional-order systems. Finally, we provide a concrete illustration of these discoveries alongside related findings. These results underscore the importance of invariant sets for local and global stability assessments in both standard and fractional-order dynamical systems. Additionally, we introduce an algorithm designed to identify invariant parabolas in planar polynomial systems. The proposed method is effective, readily understandable, and holds potential practical utility. Our key contributions lie in highlighting the prevalent role of invariant parabolas in planar system analysis and, more broadly, in showing that line and parabola subspaces are the sole invariant manifolds in fractional-order systems. These insights aid in locating invariant sets, which are essential for stability analysis. To utilize this approach, one must determine coefficients for planar polynomial systems using the proposed algorithm. However, it is critical to note that this algorithm is applicable exclusively to invariant parabolas of the specific form $vy^2+xy+wx+q=0$, where $v\neq 0$ and all other coefficients are arbitrary. This focus arises because such invariant parabolas are uniquely associated with specific polynomial expressions involving vector fields and their Jacobian matrices, a property that does not extend to other forms of invariant parabolas. Consequently, there exists a non-empty gap regarding the current understanding of invariant manifolds in planar polynomial systems, a area warranting further investigation, such as exploring invariant cubics.

This paper presents an analysis of 34 years of Arecibo data regarding PSR B1133+16, yielding high-quality dynamic spectra and their corresponding scintillation arcs generated by screens along the line of sight. We identified six distinct screens responsible for these long-lasting arcs. (QPNet), a pitch-adaptive generative model designed to enhance the limited pitch controllability of standard WaveNet (WN) through the use of pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks (PDCNNs). While WN, a probabilistic autoregressive model utilizing stacked dilated convolutions, excels at high-fidelity audio synthesis, its reliance solely on data without prior audio knowledge hampers its ability to control pitch. Specifically, WN struggles to accurately generate periodic audio components when provided with auxiliary fundamental frequency ($F_{0}$) features that fall outside the range present in the training data. To overcome these limitations, QPNet employs two innovative approaches: first, it integrates PDCNNs to dynamically adjust the WN architecture based on the input auxiliary $F_{0}$, and second, it adopts a cascaded network structure to jointly model the fundamental and harmonic components of quasi-periodic signals like speech and singing voices. Evaluations on singing voice synthesis (NSFC) and speech synthesis (NSS) demonstrate that the proposed method effectively handles unseen auxiliary $F_{0}$ values and improves perceptual qualities in both tasks. Additionally, experiments on varying auxiliary $F_{0}$ confirm the network's effectiveness in this context. Comparisons against WN and other baseline models in NSFC and NSS tasks indicate that QPNet successfully enhances the accuracy of generated fundamental frequencies and delivers more natural-sounding results. The code is accessible at https://github.com/HarryXiang/QPNet.

Our primary technical advancement demonstrates that training a network to explicitly distinguish challenging image fragments—even when the sound-emitting object is present—substantially enhances localization accuracy. We introduce a novel framework for refining bounding box annotations in the video retrieval task known as Sound-to-Sound (S2S) visible sound source localization. This dataset, titled VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS), contains over 500 video clips, each with four distinctly visible sound-emitting objects, fully annotated with bounding boxes. We demonstrate that incorporating this new dataset into the existing VGG-Sound allows our proposed algorithm to achieve state-of-the-art performance. Our approach utilizes a two-stage process: first, a initial network is trained to locate sound sources using traces of human annotation (specifically, brackets in our paper's metadata); second, a refinement network is trained using a triple mining strategy that actively selects hard samples. Experimental results on both VGG-SS and the original S2S datasets confirm the effectiveness of our method. Visual comparisons of localization results across multiple datasets and networks are also provided. The source code is available at the same URL as the abstract.

Although recent advancements in video sound source localization have largely occurred within controlled laboratory settings, significant challenges remain when applying these techniques to openly available video libraries. To address this, we developed the VGG-Sound Source (VGG-SS) dataset and a two-stage algorithm to overcome common obstacles in real-world video retrieval. To reduce annotation costs, we first trained a network using brackets as metadata to identify fragments containing visible sound sources, effectively handling occluded or distant objects. We then constructed a cost-effective two-stage network to precisely locate these sources in occluded, distant, or otherwise difficult fragments. significant recent interest. While most GCNs operate within Euclidean geometry, this approach often leads to high distortion when embedding graphs with scale-free or hierarchical structures. To address this, recent models have been developed to function in non-Euclidean spaces, particularly hyperbolic geometry. Although hyperbolic GCNs demonstrate promising results, current hyperbolic graph operations fail to strictly adhere to hyperbolic geometry, potentially limiting the space's utility and degrading model performance. This paper introduces a novel hyperbolic GCN, the Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN), which ensures that learned node features rigorously conform to hyperbolic geometry. Specifically, we reconstruct key hyperbolic graph operations, such as feature transformation and non-linear activation, using their Lorentzian counterparts. Additionally, we propose an efficient neighborhood aggregation method grounded in Lorentzian distance centroids. We further demonstrate the equivalence of these proposed operations across different types of hyperbolic geometry, providing fundamental proof of their correctness. Experiments across six datasets reveal that LGCN outperforms state-of-the-art methods and exhibits lower distortion when learning representations for tree-like graphs compared to existing hyperbolic GCNs. Furthermore, we observe that replacing standard graph operations with those defined in this paper can enhance the performance of certain existing hyperbolic GCNs. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yzhliao/LGCN.

Upon implementing this condition via the standard Faddeev-Popov procedure, the resulting gauge-fixed action retains a dependence on a single gauge parameter. This indicates that the harmonic gauge represents a family of conditions rather than a unique one. This perspective provides a physical justification for covariant harmonic gauges, which arise when a mass term is introduced for the gravitational perturbation. Specifically, selecting a particular harmonic gauge yields a theory of linearized massive gravity with the expected five degrees of freedom, successfully avoiding the vDVZ discontinuity that plagues the standard Fierz-Pauli theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the family of harmonic gauges offers an alternative approach to constructing a consistent theory of massive spin-2 particles in four spacetime dimensions by starting from linearized gauge-invariant tensors. This method yields results equivalent to those of the standard Dirac procedure applied to the massive spin-2 field. Additionally, we extend these findings to generalised harmonic gauges, drawing parallels with the theory of massive spin-1 particles. By extending the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw with the minimal dark sector, we establish a physical mechanism for neutrino oscillation lengths: the atmospheric mass scale originates from tree-level seesaw dynamics, whereas the solar scale emerges radiatively through mediation by the dark sector. Regarding the neutrino sector, we detail the structural distinctiveness of this model by contrasting it with other "missing partner" approaches; specifically, the atmospheric mass scale is generated via the standard seesaw mechanism, while the solar scale arises from effective operator dynamics. We investigate this method within the context of sentiment-guided stylization using GAN-based frameworks. The tool incorporates various statistical techniques, including standard and weighted Principal Component Analysis (PCA), elastic maps (a non-linear PCA variant), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), multilinear regression, K-Means clustering, and a decision tree algorithm variant. Featuring intuitive interfaces for customizing data point attributes (size, shape, color) and a rapid 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables users to build interactive 3D scenes representing data within multidimensional space. This allows for efficient and insightful statistical analysis, ranging from fundamental to sophisticated methods. ViDaExpert is designed as a modular system to facilitate the easy integration of new algorithms and 2D/3D visualization components. Implemented in the Python language, the library is accessible via a popular scientific package, pandas. While intended for professional statisticians and data miners, it is also suitable for educators and students of statistics. The name "ViDaExpert" is a portmanteau of Visualizing Data Expert. The library is released under the permissive GNU Public License version 3 (GPLv3). Available online at https://github.com/vi达expert/vi达expert-library, it has been utilized in various educational contexts, including a university course on multidimensional thinking for high school students learning PCA and decision trees, and a university-level module on statistical data analysis covering PCA, elastic maps, LDA, regression, clustering, and decision trees. The library also supports an introductory university course on data mining, where students gain practical experience in visualizing and analyzing real-world datasets using simple algorithms. Additionally, it is employed in a university course on statistical thinking, helping students grasp fundamental concepts of data analysis through representative cases. Beyond these examples, the library is versatile and can be applied to any straightforward "object-feature" data table with numerical values and textual labels for objects and features, such as representing countries via key indicators or images via pixel intensity values. The core components of the library are fully documented, and a well-documented sample code is also available.
